The time it takes for the $B^0_s$ meson to decay into $K^+K^-$ has an unknown average duration denoted as $\Gamma^{-1}(B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-)$. This duration is being studied by analyzing the time interval between when a $B^0_s$ meson decays and when one of its daughter kaons decays, with researchers examining a total of 337 confirmed instances of these events. By studying the relationship between the distance traveled and the momentum of the kaons, the average duration is determined to be 0.452 picometers with margins of error equal to 0.106 and 0.056 picometers. When converted into a measurable parameter, this results in $1.090$ with the same margins of error.

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a regulation problem for a physical quantity undergoing stochastic changes. The goal is to minimize the difference between a given reference function and the actual function within a specified time frame, while taking into account the associated statistical variance. To achieve this, we first establish the well-posedness of the problem in its continuous form. Furthermore, we develop and examine the existence, uniqueness, and convergence properties of a numerical approximation using a finite difference method. The convergence rate is found to be $\Delta^{1/2}$ under certain conditions.

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of annual variation in mid-to-high energy ranges. We discovered that these variations are closely aligned with the position of the Galactic center, demonstrating an annual signal matching a model of one-year periodicity with amplitude matches our expected data. Our analysis indicates that these annual shifts correspond to the movement of the Solar System in relation to a large-scale structure within our galaxy. Given the size of this structure could be estimated at a minimum of 11 kpc, this finding supports the theoretical prediction that the highest energy cosmic rays are of galactic origin.
This paper provides a proof that all Zinbiel algebras are solvable, filling in the gap left by the initial demonstration by罗 and唐 in 2012.

Researchers analyzed 502 TeV lead-lead collision data from the LHC to identify subtle variations in the angle between overlapping nuclei, which could affect the angles of emitted particles. By utilizing a newly developed method that takes into account fluctuations in the collision geometry and particle production, they found clear evidence of flow angle fluctuations and measured their impact. These fluctuations were found to be minimal, with a small effect on the overall distribution of particles. The study also found that the variation in the angle of collective flow is closely related to the variance in the transverse momentum of leaded nuclei. As well, there is a small correlation between the longitudinal flow and the transverse momentum of the produced particles.

The study of database inconsistencies has long been approached through the lens of formal dependencies, initially established by Goodman and Taylor, and later expanded upon by Chou and Kim. These dependencies are categorized into two types: those unambiguously present in all instances of a table, and those invariably absent across all table instances. Nonetheless, instances often contain ambiguous cells, which can hinder the clear identification of dependencies due to various sources of inconsistency. This research aims to expand and clarify previous work by clarifying and expanding key concepts, redefining dependencies in the presence of potential inconsistency, and introducing a novel category of dependency known as a one-sided dependency. Furthermore, the work includes an exploration of strategies to resolve inconsistencies in order to satisfy specified dependencies.

This study presents a novel dynamic statistical model called Time-Dependent Poisson Regression (TDPO) to address non-Gaussian count data that exhibits complex interdependencies and varies in its distribution over time. Building on TDPO, we have developed an advanced variant known as Time-Dependent Poisson Regression with Exogenous Regressors (TDPOX). In the TDPO model, a sequence of Poisson random variables is generated, and their interdependencies and evolving distribution are governed by a hidden Markov chain. The TDPOX model has been further enhanced to accommodate external influences on the data. We have also developed a robust statistical inference method based on the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm to estimate model parameters and conducted extensive simulations to assess model performance in various scenarios. Furthermore, we have applied the TDPO and TDPOX models to analyze real-world data sets, comparing their performance with standard statistical models.

Recent findings in object representation research have focused on encoding
portable object information into compact vectors. Such approaches provide
robustness to various forms of noise and distortion in visual data, enabling
generalization beyond the training dataset of clean images. Existing methods
achieve this by utilizing point clouds for spatially aligned reconstruction,
consequently restricting their performance to objects with negligible motion
variation, such as standing humans or stationary animals, within particular
views. In contrast, this paper presents a novel, unified object representation
that leverages the full SE(3) group to preserve object identity under any
possible transformation within the SE(3) group. By exploiting prior knowledge
of object symmetries, this method develops a descriptor field representing
both spatially invariant and equivariant information. By employing this
descriptor field, tasks like classification, detection, and multi-class
recognition can be effectively executed. Experiments conducted with the OCN
and ModelNet40 datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, yielding
significant performance gains over current state-of-the-art techniques.

A universal principle is proposed, which states that the absolute value of the Yang-Lee edge singularity $|s_0|$ should be identical for all systems that belong to the classic O(N) universality classes and exhibit three-dimensional existence. To support this hypothesis, we derive a set of one-particle operator equations that apply to the analytic continuation of the classic O(N) models in the number of components $N$. These equations are then used to calculate the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for the 3d Ising model as well as the 3d XY model with both discrete and continuous symmetry. Our results are in line with previous findings and demonstrate that despite the diverse historical approaches employed, they all yield the same result for the edge singularity position.

In statistics and machine learning, a key challenge is resolving whether to expand a suitable function within a set of estimates or whether to extend its domain of definition. An investigation of the fundamental issues underlying this "widening" versus "extension" dilemma leads to significant and contrary findings. Several examples demonstrate that the SUV inequality can arise from a "stochastic shrinking" mechanism, but, surprisingly, the opposite occurs with the Sudakov-Fernique (S-F) inequality, which stems from a "deterministic widening" principle. This result can be applied to prove the local stability of TAP free energy in a novel and concise manner. Additionally, two other functions are defined to bridge the gaps between the stochastic shrinking, widening principles, and the standard S-F inequality. These new functions may potentially serve as statistical tools for addressing the TAP fluctuations in a broader context, perhaps even beyond their current applications in mean-field theory and optimization theory.

The use of astronomy as a tool to enhance the accuracy of atmospheric monitoring, known as aerosometry, has been documented in several articles and discussions.
This paper highlights the latest developments in this area of research, with a focus on measuring the performance of super-sized air quality sensors, often called weather rocks or WaWeRrs, in a real-world environment in Reno, Nevada, and an in-depth analysis of clear-sky images taken in Antarctica using the APIS system.
These assessments demonstrate how accurate these sensors can be when it comes to detecting the precise characteristics of the atmosphere by studying the light from stars as it travels through the air.
Furthermore, research using the WaWeRRs in Antarctica has been compared to other studies and it is shown that even modest sensors can be effective in studying the unique atmosphere of Antarctica, while research with the APIS system in Antarctica has been showcased in compared clear-sky images.
Both studies also resulted in very detailed datasets that are available for researchers to use in studying the unique atmosphere of Antarctica.

Estimating the complete six-degree-of-liberty pose of non-rigid objects poses a significant challenge due to the complex internal structure that causes distorted feature representations, making it difficult to accurately predict poses using data-driven methods. Existing solutions effectively address the 3D translation and rotation aspects but failing on estimating the intricate internal deformation. This paper presents a novel deep learning framework called DeepHMap++, which leverages correspondence heatmaps to represent objects in a flattened space and employs a unique combination of projection clustering loss and correspondence learning to effectively tackle the objects' deformation. The result is an enhanced model that excels in robust and generalizable complete six-degree-of-liberty pose estimation, surpassing current methods by a large margin in prediction accuracy as demonstrated in extensive experiments.

UGLasso, GGLasso and MUGLasso are Python implementations of the Initial Value based
repeated optimization algorithm, a method introduced by Zhong et al. (2019) for solving
the Generalized Universal Graphical Lasso problem. This problem arises in the
maximum a posteriori estimation of time-varying conditional dependency structures
in multivariate time series with sparse structure prior. The repeated optimization
algorithm leverages the proximity operator's invariance property under a change of
measurement. We provide the KL-divergence-based Generalized Universal Graphical Lasso
as an illustrative example. The package supports additional likelihood functions such
as the Gaussian and Kullback-Leibler-Gaussian (GLasso), and multiple sparse structure
prior operators including the Group L1, L1, and Universal Graphical Lasso.

We introduce a robust and adaptable framework, VMD/MR-MD-Langevin, for creating and refining molecular models from atomic 3D visualizations. Although molecular models are typically refined using automated algorithms, manual adjustments remain essential, especially for complex regions like ligands. We effectively combine manual models with the Langevin Dynamics sampling method to explore molecular configurations in accordance with specified energy rules. However, existing implementations of the Langevin Dynamics method face limitations in efficiency and flexibility due to their reliance on flat-space configurational sampling. We address these issues with the VMD/MR-MD-Langevin framework, which enables the efficient sampling of molecular configurations by incorporating arbitrary mass distributions and boundary conditions. The VMD/MR-MD-Langevin method preserves the sampling efficiency and flexibility of the original Langevin Dynamics method while allowing for boundary implementations that ensure all atoms stay within a predefined volume. We demonstrate the boundary-less and hard-wall versions of our framework with end-periodic and water-box boundary conditions, respectively, and provide the source code for these implementations.

Understanding influence within group structures is essential in various contexts, be it within human societies or digital communities. A significant challenge lies in accurately assessing the influence of individual nodes, especially within multi-layered systems composed of interconnected, overlapping, and independent sub-graphs. A new approach to assessing the influence of nodes in multi-layered systems is presented, taking into consideration the relationships between nodes that are on different layers of the same system. A new concept of "importance reliance" is introduced to describe how a node's connections differ across the various systems it is a part of. A multi-layer eigenvector centrality method is developed to solve this problem, yielding a solution that indicates the level of influence of each node in the system. The usefulness of this approach is demonstrated by its application in a real-world case study of inter-connected group structures.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Berry-Romano algebra. This allows us to extend 
Dirac's equation from standard Minkowski space-time to deformed Minkowski space-time 
or $R$-Minkowski space-time. A straightforward comparison of the two extensions of 
Dirac's equation reveals an interesting deformed dispersion relation as well as 
its corresponding solution.

This research examines how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically looking at a medium speed range where a seal can form around the sphere at the water's surface. The report details different types of seals that can form, an phenomenon known as the "break-up speed," and the pressure generated as a result of the seal that can lead to water entry splashes. By using high-speed video analysis, various factors such as the sphere's partial submersion, the formation of a reverse jet, and the resulting pressure generated as a result of the seal, were analyzed. The study finds that pressure generation is most effective during the phase when the sphere is partially submerged, and that pressure generation is limited once the cavity it creates begins to oscillate. The report also highlights the tendency for spheres to generate pressure that can result in splashes, particularly around the time of break-up.

We study the moduli space of Type IIB compactifications on a Calabi-Yau four-fold with a set of four-form fluxes breaking general symmetries to a residual subset. This process results in a term analogous to a $\theta$-term in the Type IIB effective field theory, similar to that found in four-dimensional Yang-Mills theory, which is associated with the axial symmetry. This effective theory is valid when the Kaluza-Klein scale and string loop corrections can be neglected, providing a framework where we analyze the structure and implications of this $\theta$-term in four-dimensional spacetime.

Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits orbital polarization caused by a lack of equivalence in certain molecular orbitals made from 3d electrons, highlighting the need to consider potential barriers in electronic structure calculations for compounds with cubic symmetry and suggesting that cubanite is an antiorbital ordered semimetal with very low mobility electrons.

The behavior of excitons, particles that are electrically neutral, is influenced by their interactions, even in the presence of no external magnetic field. When an external magnetic field is applied, the particles exhibit a wide range of phenomena, such as giant orbital magnetic dipole fluctuations. In this research, we report on the discovery of extremely large Rabi frequency fluctuations reaching as high as 100% in quantum dark exciton pairs under the influence of a no external magnetic field. This finding is supported by both theoretical predictions and experimental evidence, which reveal that the fluctuations are caused by asymmetric shape fluctuations in GaAs quantum dots. In the absence of an external magnetic field, these quantum dark exciton fluctuations enable a better understanding and management of dexciton physics.

We are interested in analyzing a two-dimensional wallpaper network lattice that exhibits non-symmorphic properties and we are ignoring spin-orbit coupling effects. Using this model, we are able to demonstrate the formation of cone-shaped band structures at the high-symmetry $\Gamma$ point at the center of the Brillouin zone. We further show that by making specific adjustments, we can move these band structures from the $\Gamma$ point to other locations within the Brillouin zone or even cause them to overlap at the vertical mirror line. We also establish that non-symmorphic symmetry results in mirror band structures across the vertical mirror line, and we confirm these findings through analytical and numerical analyses.

Quantum phase measurements are highly valuable in a wide range of applications including sensor technology and fundamental research. Recently, it was shown that a certain type of quantum phase that's infinitesimally small can be used as a resource in certain processes. We investigate the characteristics of this catalyzed phase in the context of Mach-Zehnder interferometry. It was found that this phase is directly, and consistently, proportional to the photon number it affects, and it's also indicative of a form of extreme sensitivity to pressure that's comparable to that of coherent oscillations but occurs at much lower photon energies. We also provide and discuss an experimental method to measure this catalyzed phase.

In General Relativity, the Newman-Penrose formalism has several distinct features. One approach involves using a tetrad of null vectors, which we will demonstrate using the Python-based `sage` software through the Bivector package. We will explore the 18 complex Newman-Penrose scalars that can be calculated from the tensor field of the electromagnetic Weyl and Ricci curvatures. We will specifically analyze the conditions under which these scalars become zero, which leads to a classification of vacuum spacetimes based on the Weyl curvature, referred to as the "Weyl curvature simplex."

A recent framework proposed by Gaston and Acampora (2019) effectively captures the composition of complex polymers by using a concatenation of simpler polymers and basic chemical elements. This framework represents both the complex and simple polymers as draws from an alphabet of chemical elements, consisting of integers representing the elements' positions in the periodic table. To determine the elements in a complex polymer, previously attempted methods like solving a system of nonlinear equations have met limited success. However, by approximating this system of equations with an integer version, we were able to successfully apply a combination of statistical techniques, including non-negative regression, and optimization methods, such as mixed integer linear programming, to accurately infer the composition of multiple complex polymers. This was demonstrated through the inference of the composition of DNA based on its constituent simple polymers (DNA bases) and elements (chemical periodic table).

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very challenging, especially when the scans are noisy or images are incomplete. To compensate for these issues, deep learning models have been developed to improve the accuracy of segmenting tumors in CT scans. Most current models, based on deep learning, rely on loss functions and data augmentation techniques to enhance the segmentation results. However, this paper argues that enhancing the feature extraction capability of the base deep learning architecture, rather than relying solely on loss functions and data augmentation, would be more effective. To illustrate this point, multiple approaches have been developed to improve the extraction of features. According to the methodology proposed in this paper, the original Unet model has been enhanced by incorporating three distinct components: dense connections, attention mechanisms, and dilated convolutions. Consequently, the proposed DDAUnet model combines all three components into a single framework with the hope of improving the segmentation of tumors in the esophagus from CT scans. To validate the proposed methodology, experiments have been conducted using the two commonly used datasets, leading to the result where the proposed DDAUnet model has surpassed the original Unet model and other comparable models in terms of segmentation accuracy.

Multilingual individuals frequently use a combination of two or more languages, known as code-switching or code-mixing, in their written and spoken communication. Despite its significant implication in the field of multilingual natural language processing, research in this area has primarily focused on either adjacent languages with shared vocabulary or non-adjacent languages with little vocabulary overlap, ignoring a large spectrum of intermediate overlap scenarios. In this paper, a comprehensive literature review of code-mixing data and models is presented, highlighting various challenges and factors influencing model performance, including the concept of "anchor language." Moreover, several promising future research directions are identified, including an exploration of three understudied code-mixing scenarios: intra-language mixing, community-specific mixing, and mixing of related dialects. The author calls for standardized benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics in this field, particularly one that aligns with the unique characteristics of the Filipino linguistic community.

Evaluating automated descriptions, such as those generated for images, videos, and search results, has traditionally relied on human-written references. However, we've found that using annotated datasets like WikiAttributes and Facebook's BAbI to assess descriptions for images is fundamentally flawed. Our study reveals that these datasets are unsuitable benchmarks for images due to their distinct creation processes, comprising a mix of machine-generated and human-written descriptions, and contain numerous inaccuracies. Consequently, we found that humans' ability to verify the correctness of descriptions is severely limited, and human performance on tasks requiring accurate world knowledge is significantly poorer than previously assumed. Our findings highlight the critical need to re-examine and replace current methods for evaluating descriptions generated for images, videos, and web search results.

Ta$_2$O$_5$ is a highly complex lattice material with a polymeric structure, making it an underutilized candidate for various optical applications. To understand and potentially exploit the interesting properties of Ta$_2$O$_5$ lattice state, research was conducted using a combination of first-principles and Monte Carlo simulations. Our findings reveal that the ta$_2$o$_5$ ground state exhibits a second-order Jahn-Teller effect, resulting in a unique hybridization of Ta-O bonds and explaining its unusually high optical band gap. Surprisingly, the ta$_2$o$_5$ ground state demonstrates a lower total energy compared to the widely recognized Ta$_2$O$_5$ monoclinic structure, despite having a wider optical band gap. Furthermore, research found that the ta$_2$o$_5$ ground state exhibits a $145$ eV lattice spacing, making it significantly harder to detect experimentally due to its exceptionally small probability of occurrence.

Previous studies on the spread of information within online social networks have been hindered by the difficulty in comparing results across different countries of the United States due to the varying sizes and online populations of states. A new approach breaks across this limitation by utilizing the Migration Policy Institute's definition of a large geographic shift to identify 59 metropolitan areas that underwent significant population movement between 2008 and 2017 within the same region. Leveraging Reddit's discussions on migration in metropolitan areas during 2017, our research investigates the impact of population movement on the spread of information, focusing on 17 U.S. metropolitan areas. We utilize a gravity model of information circulation, controlling for the size and development of each metropolitan area, to find the following key discoveries: (1) the spread of information does not always follow the development or size of a metropolitan area; (2) more developed and larger areas do not necessarily have lower barriers to information circulation; and and (3) there is a wide variation in the effect of population movement on the spread of information among similar metropolitan areas, possibly due to factors such as the presence of online social media in new arrivals' backgrounds, the integration of migrants into local communities, and the accuracy of population migration data.

Humans frequently employ verbal guidance to assist robots in completing various activities, and this study dissects such verbal demonstrations by breaking them into components such as speech timing, the choice of commands, and vocal tone. A group of eight humans carried out a manipulation task for a robot, which involved reading instructions from a computer, and their guidance were recorded and analyzed. The study created three main conditions to examine: the content of the instructions, changes in vocal tone, and instructions delivered in varying tempos under both ideal and challenging listening conditions. The results show that instructions tend to be spoken clearly and at a moderate pace, with less emphasis on tone and more content-focused instructions being particularly helpful for the robot. Furthermore, more modulations in vocal tone and increased speech pace under difficult listening conditions could enhance the robot's understanding. The findings of this study can be applied to automatically assessing verbal demonstrations and designing effective training methods for verbal guidance.

A novel set of differential equations is derived to model the intricate behavior in 2D conformal field theory, offering a differential equation approach to study the complex correlations in the theory. These equations are identified as a broader category of Euler-Arnold equations, which, after a specific transformation, reduce to the Painleve-III equation under certain parameters. A particular aspect of this relationship is that the coefficients of the Euler-Arnold equations correspond to the conformal data of the theory. Furthermore, this connection enables us to generate non-trivial solutions for the complex correlations of multiple primary fields in the theory.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these
interfaces are continuously improving. However, the speed of development for
these systems outpaces the advancement in automated testing. This discrepancy
results in a higher risk of failures affecting users. To bridge this gap, our
research focuses on automated testing for a class of systems with conversational
interfaces. Our method involves automated systems that can independently
evaluate the performance of the conversational agents. In contrast to previous
methods, our automated testing framework yields improvements in three key areas:
it produces more effective detected anomalies, allows for the discovery of issues
deeper in the system's processing, and requires minimal input from developers.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Multi-sparse-domain cooperative recommendation (MSDR), a novel subcategory of cross-domain recommendation, aims to leverage the limited data across multiple sparse domains to enhance the accuracy of recommendations. Despite substantial progress in cross-domain recommendations, the problem of multi-sparse-domer cooperative recommendation remains underexplored. Current multi-domain recommendation models are constrained by their requirement for complete user data across all domains. In contrast, in multi-sparse-domer settings, users may provide data across only a subset of the domains. To address this challenge, we propose a novel recommendation framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation via Enhanced Comprehensive Aspect Preference Learning (MSD-CAP). This framework comprises two key components: a Enhanced Comprehensive Aspect Preference Learning module that leverages a set of dense domains to predict user preferences in underrepresented domains, and a Knowledge Augmentation module that fills in missing information for users with absent data in certain domains. Experimental evaluations on three real-world datasets confirm the superior performance of our proposed MSD-CAP over multiple baseline models.

Convex optimization issues often utilize various conic formulations to achieve better performance and efficiency. In the realm of conic optimizations, prominent cones such as the positive semidefinite cone and the ice cream cone are well-established. However, lesser-known cones like the linear elasticity cone, the ordered three-fold symmetric cone, and the blowfly cone lack widespread application. We introduce a Natural Conic Solver built on the Hypatia solver manifold that facilitates the application of these specialized cones to real-world problems by performing a coordinate transformation. This research highlights a few key examples where employing exotic conic formulations can be beneficial. In addition, our BPR-Elasticity software demonstrates a practical application of the elasticity cone in solving recommendation system problems via method transfer.

The rapid progression of MRI technology and artificial intelligence relies on high-quality datasets, yet even experienced radiologists face difficulties in consistently assessing data quality due to the subtle and sometimes deceptive artifacts produced by MRI errors. This paper presents a new, end-to-end neural network approach that learns from the inconsistent assessments of multiple experts' opinions and applies this knowledge to flag images with significant defects. Our method effectively identifies a range of common MRI distortions, including aliasing, motion blurring, and various types of noise, across diverse image protocols such as T1-weighted and T2-weighted images. Experiments show that our system's performance in detecting faulty images closely matches that of human experts, with a CUP score of 0.75 compared to 0.73 for the best radiological model, and it also demonstrates strong generalization across different image protocols without retraining. Furthermore, our system proves to be highly efficient in flagging bad images, with a 200 times faster processing speed than the top radiological model, making it a practical and versatile quality control tool for MRI data.

The resilience of the electrical grid is increasingly influenced by private electric vehicles, yet this factor has seen little research attention. Widespread EV usage has the potential to both support and stress the electrical network, depending on how they are managed and utilized during both regular operations and events causing outages. This research aims to explore and address the complexity of EV interactions with distribution networks by presenting an innovative idea where private EV owners use an optimization approach to decide on charging and discharging patterns, with the primary goal of minimizing electricity costs and, as a result, enhancing their overall comfort levels. Furthermore, the EV owners' decisions are influenced by network events, and we employ a multi-agent simulation to investigate the effectiveness of this concept, comparing it to traditional automatic charging methods and highlighting the significance of considering resilience in the design of future EV management strategies.

The challenge of multi-agent conversation has been extensively studied using the single-agent repetition task as a foundation, yet achieving a high success rate in multi-agent conversation remains a significant achievement compared to the single-agent version. To bridge the gap between the single and multi-agent versions of the repetition task, we propose a novel drive-based motivation approach that enables agents to determine when to repeat information or speak independently. Although simple in concept, this approach results in agents exhibiting repetitive behavior and successfully completing the conversation task with high consistency. Nevertheless, our method's success rate lags behind more advanced methods that utilize a model to predict the repetition necessity. Consequently, future research could explore incorporating the concept of drive with these advanced methods to enhance their robustness and reliability.

This study employs an ab initio approach to investigate the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3. We utilize a total energy minimization strategy within the JDFT code to determine the most stable crystal structure of these materials, and then apply the Blandé-Sankey method to analyze their electronic and magnetic behavior. Our findings reveal that GdSn3 and CmSn3 exhibit the ZnS-b1 structure in their most stable phase, and both materials display itinerant magnetism with a total magnetic moment of 7.00 $\mu_B$ per formula unit, in accordance with the Fermi's theorem for GdSn3. Notably, CmSn3 exhibits slight semi-conducting behavior with a band gap of 0.04 eV. Moreover, the GdxCm1-xSn3 series retains the ZnS-b1 structure and demonstrates identical magnetic behavior to GdSn3, with a total magnetic moment of 7.00 $\mu_B$ per formula unit for all values of x.

Using forecasts from the AGILE, Fermi-LAT, and DAMPE space missions, potential 
additional contributions from dark matter annihilation or decay are examined in the 
gamma-ray band, complementing existing reviews in other areas. By utilizing the CTDM 
dark matter haloe model, the evidence for dark matter from observations of the galactic 
centre and the whole galaxy is assessed, considering both the total gamma-ray signal 
and the spectral characteristics. Furthermore, the ability of space-based experiments 
to detect dark matter signals from individual star clusters and the Milky Way's 
disc is assessed, highlighting where current space experiments stand and what future 
missions could achieve.

For any finite reflection group $W$, let $\Sigma$ be the set of associated reflections and consider the Coxeter group $B_n$ with its set of generators reflected in the Coxeter graph. If there is a finite set $S$ that contains $\Sigma$, then according to the "foundation theorem" from BAAD presentation theory, $W$ has an exact "foundation" presentation relative to $B_n$, which means the relations defining the Coxeter graph are complete for $W$. Nevertheless, when the Coxeter graph is of type $D$, this is not the case and $W$ cannot be considered as having a direct relationship with the set $S$. This paper presents an improvement to this result by showing that $W$ has a modified "foundation" presentation, which means there is a precise correspondence between the "foundation" presentation and the well-known additional relation that defines $W$.

We investigated weak lensing effects on the observed distribution of Type Ia supernovae in a large sample consisting of 650 galaxies. By analyzing a plot of supernovae concentrations versus their colors from the Pantheon dataset, we identified a boundary above which supernovae in highly dense galaxies tend to appear brighter. This boundary aligns with predictions from cosmological simulations of lensing effects. Furthermore, we discovered a distinct separation between supernovae in spiral and elliptical galaxies when plotting their stellar surface density. Supernovae in spiral galaxies were largely found in less dense regions, whereas supernovae in elliptical galaxies were predominantly located in more dense regions. There was also a correlation between the supernovae's observed magnitudes and their host galaxy densities that is independent of the distribution of intrinsic supernovae luminosities. This observed effect weak lensing contributes to is comparable in magnitude to the effect dark energy has on the same distance scale.

This paper introduces a novel optical component called the T-junction and explores its properties and applications in integrated photonic systems. A breakdown of the scattering process that occurs within T-junctions is presented, highlighting how angle and bending radius can influence integrated circuit performance. A comparative analysis is provided between T-junctions and 90-degree bends, demonstrating that they produce similar loss results under identical conditions. Additionally, a design for a symmetric 90-degree bend utilizing two back-to-back T-junctions is discussed.

A new object detection method, Mask R-CNN context object classification, has been developed and shows promising results in various tasks. In this study, we investigate the underlying mechanisms of the detector's ability to utilize context by utilizing 10,583 instances of the COCO detector on the AIR dataset. Our analysis includes visual and statistical examinations of misclassified objects in relation to correctly classified ones. We discovered that accurately classified objects are more likely to be clearly visible, fully contained within the image, and associated with contextual objects, in contrast to those that are misclassified. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating object scores into the RPN stage significantly boosts performance, and we propose an alternative context-aware detector that achieves comparable results to Mask R-CNN context object classification.

We examine and refine-certain inequalities for strongly negatively associated binary random variables, building on the work of Kuelbs and Rachev in 1990. This investigation develops concentration inequalities for functions of such variables, extends an inequality from Gilat in 2009 for independent binary random variables, and generalizes another inequality from Liu and Wang in 2013. Specifically, we prove the following inequality for a smooth function $f$ and $n$ strongly negatively associated binary random variables $x_n$: $\mathbb{P}\left(f(x_n)-\mathbb{E}f(x_n) \geq t\right) \leq \exp\left(\frac{t^2}{s_n^2}\right)$, where $s_n^2 \leq \sum_{i=1}^{n} \text{Var}(x_i^i)$. This result holds for all $t > 0$ and we also establish a similar inequality for lower tails of such functions. Furthermore, we establish inequalities for the tail probabilities of the sum of independent uniform random vectors, the number of closed paths in a acyclic graph, and the Riemann zeta-function.

For any two non-degenerate quadratic forms Q and P over a specific region U in R^n, we define a novel concept known as the "symplectic conversion" involving the incorporation of definite quadratic forms. This concept is an alternative to isotopy and generally holds under a broader set of conditions. We investigate the properties of "symplectic conversion," establish its fundamental theorems, and provide an applied example in general position Lagrangian immersion.

We analyzed the transplant acceptance policies for fully HLA-matched kidneys from deceased donors without volunteers. A specific category of recipients, eligible to receive these kidneys but not volunteers themselves, was identified. Statistical data from the US allows for the evaluation of a transfusion-free rejection-minimizing approach. The results indicate that implanting these kidneys has the potential to save approximately 30 lives per year in the US, whereas the current approach leads to approximately 80 failed transplants annually. Notably, this approach may offer these recipients a path to becoming volunteers for a matched kidney donor.

This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing the presence of an orthogonal basis that can be computed using singular value decomposition (SVD). This basis structure is validated through numerical experiments utilizing the Loughran-McDonald sentiment dataset. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of our model's insights to a range of practical tasks, including reordering the dimensions of NLP embeddings to isolate words with heightened levels of ambiguity and extracting specific word attributes through linear combinations. Doeringer et al.'s (2020) initial exploration forms the foundation of our research, which aims to expand the understanding of NLP embeddings' limitations and potential applications.

This paper extends the concepts introduced in [1] to SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based waveforms, achieving extra gain from multiple transmit antennas and multiple subcarriers in energy transfer and data transmission. Employing an effectiveness map, we visualize the space of receiver distances and frequencies where the energy and data gain from wideband waveforming is significant, and provide insights into when wideband waveforming is beneficial over traditional DFS-based frequency access. Furthermore, we derive the energy and data gain from wideband waveforming in the far-field and near-field regions, and demonstrate the accuracy of these approximations through numerical results.

This study develops and analyses an numerical method to model the interaction between a solid and liquid phase in one dimension, taking into account latent heat and non-monotone interface energy per unit area. A hybrid level-set / embedded boundary approach is employed to achieve this, with a partially linearized level-set method used to track the interface and a finite element method applied to solve the governing heat equation on the given domain. The interface is then shifted by incorporating an additional energy term into the discretization. The proposed scheme maintains maximum $L^\infty$ accuracy for temperature, with a interface position accuracy of maximum $L^1$ accuracy of 3.0 delta t and a mass conservation capability. The proposed scheme also includes a interface barrier to prevent the interface from exceeding the maximum allowed distance. Numerical experiments are conducted in order to demonstrate the method's effectiveness, including a treatment of a repeated melt-solidification process on a one-dimensional domain, implicit in the previous approach.

We introduce a learning method that produces a tree-based explanation structure for a multiplayer game by iteratively refining a set of hypothesis trees through the examination of players' actions at various tree nodes. This approach enables a tree to be utilized for both predictive purposes and to provide human-readable rationale for each player's behavior at each decision point. We refine our hypothesis by identifying players' actions that deviate significantly from the norm, taking into consideration both the frequency and magnitude of these actions. We conduct a series of experiments with multiple reinforcement learning agents engaged in repeated multiplayer games, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method in capturing relevant information for predicting player behavior at each tree node, while also providing more concise and accurate explanations compared to existing linear model-based approaches.

An analysis of a model for an SIR epidemic on a randomly constructed dynamic network shows an extensive outbreak can be effectively avoided by strategically connecting to new clusters if the infection rate is sufficiently high. The study also investigates the impact of a varying network connection rate on cluster sizes and critical infection rates, finding higher rates result in smaller clusters and an increased critical rate. A proposed model's predictions were accurately validated through Monte Carlo simulations.

A new methodology is proposed to incorporate latest data into the Parton Distribution Function (PDF) sets, building upon the traditional DGLAP evolution framework. The proposed approach extends this framework by integrating initial conditions at a specific scale with a theoretical parameter that can be fine-tuned to align the PDF set with various factorization scales. The resulting parameters are directly comparable to those in the PDF space, providing a direct link between the Parton Density and the Hadron. The proposed framework is implemented in the root-based PDF fitting tool, and an application of this framework yields parameters to be incorporated into the CT18 PDF set, based on the $\gamma p$ data. The framework is generally applicable to other hadrons as well, and is intended to be continuously updated in line with new data, more precise calculations, and advanced fitting techniques.

For policies to effectively generalize across new data, it's crucial for them to consistently decrease the residual errors, also known as the backup signal. This paper investigates the impact of experience replay on long-horizon decision problems by analyzing a finite experience buffer, and reveals that optimal policies from infinite experience buffers achieve a desirable property called Variance Diminution (VD). This Property helps overcome the extensive state space limitations imposed by pure supervised learning. We then introduce a limited experience buffer algorithm, Value-Experience Replay (VER), which maximizes the state space capabilities by exploiting the Variance Diminution (VD) principle, and achieves the same sample efficiency as Tree Search with Prioritised Experience Replay (TPER) in settings with an infinite experience buffer, and with Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (MBER) when the experience buffer is restricted. We have validated our theoretical findings and improved performance on MuJoCo tasks.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue construction, we developed MultiTalk, a vast and diverse dialogue tree comprising 55,595 spoken sentences across 415 distinct conversation paths. Existing dialogue datasets, including those commonly used for modeling, typically revolve around circular conversations with limited diversity. In contrast, our annotated data features multi-turn exchanges, intricate knowledge-driven inquiries, anacronistic discussions, and multi-way questioning, offering a significantly more complex environment for research. High-branching dialogue data like MultiTalk presents an opportunity to enhance the efficiency of conversational model training by reducing the size of these expansive dialogue trees. We recommend employing selective sampling techniques to curate compact and representative dialogues, maintaining adequate context while preserving the unique characteristics of the original dialogue tree. Our experimental evaluations indicate that the most effective context context contexts to retain are those that minimize reconstruction losses, guiding the development of automatic dialogue construction methods. Additionally, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of using dialogue trees in a down-stream task, specifically classification, yielding substantial performance gains over circular conversations.

We present our package MGfast-jupyter, a set of tools enabling rapid exploration and fine-tuning of N-body simulation code for cosmological gravitational theories, specifically designed for investigating modified gravity models. Our package includes the capability to readily produce mock observations and facilitate the testing of data analysis methods and statistical tests for distinguishing between general relativity and alternative gravitational theories. To streamline modified gravity simulations, we developed a set of tools that allow for efficient implementation of multiple complex models within the N-body simulation code by modifying a single input file. Our package is demonstrated using lambda CDM and two specific modified gravity models: T5 and T6.

The connection between the sub-Gaussian analytic functions and the stochastic Loewner evolution has been established for a single particle system; now this relationship is independently valid for one particle as well as multi-particle systems. In this research, we investigate the drive of the SLE equation's coefficient by the position of particles in the upper half-plane, either with interaction or not, and these systems yield the same result for the Gaussian free field on the half-plane up to null sets. The research paper builds on the work of multiple authors, including Beffara, Smart, Werner, and others.

Collaborative projects that involve compiling knowledge through input from multiple contributors are being more frequently seen in areas such as software development with git-based collaborations, and knowledge construction with platforms like Wikipedia. To accomplish complex, cross-authorship scientific projects that entail both reading and writing knowledge, a scribe-like method of collaboration is common in scientific projects, accompanied by tools such as Overleaf for real-time group editing. However, this type of collaboration is challenging in fields like neuroscience research when dealing with large datasets that require a substantial amount of data from multiple authors when presented in formats like Jupyter notebooks. To address these challenges, we introduced a highly flexible and easy-to-use collaborative platform called WorkingWiki derived from MediaWiki software, allowing for real-time multi-author note-taking and knowledge construction that mirrors the PLOS Anatomy Anatomy Atlas project in neuroscience research.

This study uses a method linearized to better understand the reaction of a turbulent jet flame to acoustic vibrations in an acoustically resonant chamber. We utilize an active flame model, which simulates the flame's reaction to vibrations by adjusting the fuel flow based on a prescribed phase angle. This phase angle approach replaces the need for a feedback control mechanism typically used in research. By generating a series of numerical simulations of turbulent jet flames, we aim to identify the key parameters that define the flame's reaction to these vibrations. The study's parameters include the phase angle, the level of turbulence in the jet, the intensity of the vibrations, and the geometry of the chamber. The resulting data provides a predictive framework for understanding and controlling reaction of turbulent jet flames in the context of acoustic vibrations.

We analyzed the implications of neutrinos interacting with ultralit dark matter, specifically the scale production of dark matter and neutrino free-streaming's delay due to this interaction. The degree to which this interaction hinders neutrino free-streaming can be measured by a dimensionless interaction strength parameter, and we explored the resulting limits on the neutrino mass and the scale of ultralight dark matter. The study of $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay duration provides an upper limit on the effective neutrino mass, offering a constraint that must be compared and potentially could offer evidence for dark matter if it occurs in the ultralight range. In addition, cosmic microwave background and large scale structure observations provide further restrictive conditions on the theory. Based on these analyses, and given current experimental sensitivities to the $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay, we found that this interaction could lead to the production of ultralight dark matter with a mass around $10^{-22} \textrm{ eV}$ at most, assuming a neutrino majorana mass of approximately 1 MeV.

In the context of nonlocal gravity theories, a precise definition of the fundamental frames is essential for formulating a nonlocal relationship between these frames and the metric frame. This metric relationship serves as a constitutive relation that forms the basis of the field equations in the geometric formulation of nonlocal gravity theories. A comparative analysis of two prominent models, the $f(R,\Box) $ gravity and the $f(G,T) $ gravity, highlights the significance of defining the fundamental frames. In both models, we derive the constitutive relations and provide a systematic approach to solving the field equations. As an illustrative example, we discuss the solution for the metric in a spherically symmetric setup within the framework of $f(G,T) $ gravity.

We combined the results from genome-wide association studies with an advanced statistical model to assess the functionality of genomic elements, using 18 human traits as examples. This combined approach revealed that associated variants found in studies are heavily concentrated in specific functional categories. Traits were also found to differ significantly in terms of which genomic elements are relevant, and variations in gene density were shown to impact the distribution of associated variants. Additionally, some species that are extinct had complex relationships with certain human traits, and we discovered that some associations between humans and other species could be explained by shared genomic features, while others remained unexplained due to the uniqueness of those species' biology. Furthermore, some of the results from this study were validated using a different method, and various findings were illustrated visually using 2100 associations across the 18 human traits.

This paper presents an overview of research on small systems conducted at the LHC, focusing on experiments with protons and electrons electrons colliding at high energies. The abundance of data obtained from small systems enables the examination of collective phenomena and jet quenching, previously thought to be exclusive to heavy ion collisions. The paper delves into open questions regarding small systems, leveraging insights from heavy ion collisions to potentially gain a deeper understanding. It highlights the value of small systems in heavy ion collisions, particularly in exploring the initial state, jet quenching, and thermal radiation. The paper also discusses the utility of small systems as a tool in heavy ion collisions, by comparing results from small systems embedded within heavy ion collisions to those from small systems in isolation. It emphasizes the importance of electron-ion collisions for small system studies, presenting unique opportunities offered by eOH and sCH processes. The paper draws on recent research and theoretical predictions to advance our knowledge of small systems.

Recent observations from the Rubin LSST and the Euclid space telescope have highlighted the necessity to understand the recurrence patterns of neutron star X-ray binary transients in the Milky Way. A new study uses simple physics and previous data from the 2MASS and X-ray databases of the Milky Way to test two primary theories explaining the recurrence intervals of these transients located in the galaxy. According to both models, a binary system containing a neutron star can undergo multiple outbursts before the Inacive Accretion Disc eventually expels the system. If most of these transients occur as result of accretion, then their recurrence rates would be determined by the distribution of binary systems in the galaxy, and a set of algorithms were developed to simulate their behavior. Conversely, if they result from the disruption of planets or brown dwarfs around the neutron stars, then an incomplete set of equations based on past observations from the Sgr A* X-ray cluster was employed to simulate one-dimensional recycling cycles. Both models predict that the majority of these transients have recurrence rates of less than a few hundred thousand years, and thus, it is proposed that the X-ray transients located in the Sgr A* cluster and the typical quiescent X-ray binaries in the Milky Way may be found by conducting large-scale optical and near-infrared sky surveys.

We derived and applied a novel expansion of the ionized impact operator under the assumption that both the electron and proton are limited to a narrow range of momenta. This expansion comprises three distinct terms: one is proportional to the displacement of the ionic potential, another is an expansion of the electronic Hamiltonian, and the third is linear in the momentum operator and responsible for a unique spin-phonon interaction absent in previous theories. Our electron-phonon and spin-phonon expansion coefficients are demonstrated to be applicable to a variety of trions and excitons with the help of solid-state and trapped ion models.

The exploration of Natural Language Understanding (NLU) in informal conversations is hindered by the semantic variability of language in dialogue contexts. This paper investigates the source of this semantic variability by employing a Natural Language Inference (NLI) task to analyze spoken conversations. The study consists of two parts: a semantic diversity evaluation model is proposed that integrates an NLI assumption, and the resulting dataset is introduced as a secondary contribution. Both components are consistently evaluated using a subset of the Isaac corpus. Furthermore, this is compared to the results from an NLI-assessment without any prior assumption. Findings suggest that the previously proposed universal assumption leads to substantial diversity among speech acts, but this effect is not as pronounced as the variation found when using an NLI-assumption. Additionally, the NLI-assessment is found to introduce significant diversity when applied to a synthetic dataset with randomly assigned semantics, thus confirming its suitability for assessing semantic variability.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rotation. Computer calculations model rotating low-mass stars with the ability for sustained hydrogen energy production, considering a range of rotation speeds, masses, and angular momentum conservation during collapse. However, these models predict that stars that are close to the critical rotation speed would prevent sustainable hydrogen burning above a certain mass threshold. Although models lack the capacity to accurately represent the physics of radiative rotation diffusion and prograde instabilities, evidence has been found suggesting that even a slowly rotating star could be unstable to convection. As the speed of rotation increases, the conditions under which the star becomes unstable to the Coriolis force and centrifugal force occur. As a result, the relationship between the critical rotation speed and the angular velocity that triggers convection is influenced.

The task of creating amplitude analysis tools has been driven by the interest in
reconstructing particle interactions from data. Traditionally, these models began with
the Wigner's recurrence relationship to incorporate angular momentum constraints,
followed by the incorporation of partial data, such as Dalitz plots. Now, the need
is expanding, as these analyses also demand the inclusion of external particle
relationships, specifically the masses of constituent particles, in addition to their
momenta. This paper explores the development of recurrent models suitable for such
analyses, with a particular emphasis on addressing the effects of these external
relationships and presenting various approaches to this challenge.

Dynamic evolution of interstellar medium has significant impact on light
propagation and particle interactions, which in turn affects afterglow light curves.
Dark galactic disk, low density halo, and high velocity cluster are three
standard models of the local interstellar medium, but they fail to comprehensively
explain light curve observations from all scenarios. As a result, new standard
model, consisting of two phases - a transparent, low-density outer phase and an
opaque, high-density inner phase- has been proposed to better explain afterglow
observations. However, evidence for this model is still predominantly anecdotal
rather than solid. In order to address this issue, we developed a new simulation
that incorporates this two-phase model, and found that it includes all three
scenarios of the proposed new standard model. Our simulation demonstrates that
dynamic evolution of the two-phase model leads to a predictable pattern of light
curve residuals that can be used to diagnose models of the interstellar medium,
which in turn provides a systematic way to study the local interstellar medium.

Bipartite graphs with no odd cycles longer than k can have their larger part reduced by splitting at most a constant number of vertices, where the constant is dependent on the maximum odd cycle length. This is in contrast to non-planar graphs, where the constant is one, and tree-width is equal to the maximum odd cycle length plus two.

This paper is named "Thruster-Assisted Bipedal Locomotion for Greater Efficiency and Reliability" and it aims to present several advancements made to the previously published bipedal robot, which naturally returns to its upright position after being pushed aside and recovers from being overturned with minimal loss of momentum.

We define valued domains in contrast to Tate rings and demonstrate that, given any valuation ring V embedded in a domain D with a specific property, the associated valued domain remains equivalent to the original. Furthermore, we establish criteria for when a valued domain converts back into a Tate ring. However, it's proven that the valued ring associated with a Tate ring is not always the same as the original, even under various separation axioms. Additionally, we identify a condition where the valued ring of a Tate ring is fully exchangeable with the original. Notably, we show that no valued domain exists within the category of local rings or rings with a topology. Finally, we provide a characterized set of conditions for a valued domain to be exchangeable with a Tate ring.

In response to shrinking improvements in multicore processors, hyper-threading, and overclocking, we propose HyperDegrade, a novel hyper-threading-based technique for enhancing multiple processes by simultaneously lowering the CPU's processes' frequencies. By efficiently utilizing underused CPU resources, hyper-threading enables us to simultaneously lower the frequencies of multiple processes while simultaneously managing them without any interference. Our simultaneous frequency management strategy concurrently modifies the processes' frequencies by determining the optimal degree of modification that can be applied to the processor. We implemented HyperDegrade on top of Linux and it consumes nearly negligible system resources. In a controlled test, we discovered that HyperDegrade is capable of simultaneously lowering the CPU's processes' frequencies up to 12 times more than the current solutions. Moreover, in real-world scenarios, HyperDegrade consumes almost no system resources, while the current techniques consume 2.9 GHz of CPU efficiency.

We introduce a novel link operation known as the swap, which can be understood in the context of classical links as follows: given two links that interlace in a specific region of 3D space, we can reverse their orientation in the plane they occupy by crossing them, and this alteration results in an equivalent link under certain conditions. We then investigate the invariance of the Kauffman bracket and the Jones polynomial under the swap, and it is established that both remain unchanged. Furthermore, the swap remains consistent when applied to welded links, and its impact on the Kauffman bracket and the Kauffman polynomial is also examined.

We demonstrate that the Fox-Hatcher loop, which is known to be non-trivial in the free group with three generators, is in fact trivial within the second stem of the rational homotopy groups of spheres. This result is in contrast to a general pattern established previously, where all non-trivial loops are situated starting from the fifth stem. Our finding is part of a broader class of exceptions to this pattern.

This paper addresses the development of a synchronized control strategy for a group of robots performing diverse duties. Unlike previous studies that focused on synchronized synchronization, our approach examines a controlled synchronization method for these robots to efficiently execute their various activities within limited synchronization time frames. The performance of the proposed strategy is evaluated using simulated scenarios, comparing limited and optimal synchronization methods to demonstrate its effectiveness in improving overall system productivity.
