The occurrence of a single event causing widespread infection is known as a super-spreader event. These incidents, although rare, have the potential to provide valuable insights and should not be overlooked. This study delves into the dynamics of a single super-spreader event, taking into account various factors such as environmental conditions, host behavior, and pathogen characteristics. The research utilizes an SIR model and Monte Carlo simulations to analyze the spread of the disease. The results demonstrate that, in addition to the well-documented rapid transmission, super-spreader events can also result in the introduction of the pathogen to new populations through importation infections. The concept of a "window period" is proposed, marking the time following the event when heightened infection risks give way to normal levels. The analysis further highlights the intricate relationship between risk windows of different populations and offers implications for disease control and prevention, emphasizing the importance of breaking the transmission chain during this period. The research also calls upon the scientific community to actively seek opportunities to study real-world super-spreader events.

Let V be a complex topological vector space. We define a cyclic set of operators on V as a collection $\Omega$ consisting of continuous linear operators on V, where the smallest subspace of V that is invariant under the action of $\Omega$ is dense within V. If the smallest invariant subspace of V under $\Omega$ is V itself, we refer to $\Omega$ as a coregular set of operators on V. The properties and characteristics of cyclic and coregular sets of operators on V are examined in this study. The research reveals that a single operator is cyclic precisely when it is regular, and also demonstrates that any weakly algebraically irreducible single operator is both cyclic and algebraically irreducible. Additionally, the research establishes the following properties for a set $\mathcal{A}$ of operators on V: (1) any subset of a coregular set of operators is cyclic; (2) any superset of a cyclic set of operators is cyclic, provided the superset shares the same common kernel and common range intersection; (3) any set of operators that contains the complex scalar field as a subset is cyclic; and (4) any commutative set of algebraically irreducible operators is both cyclic and algebraically irreducible.

A study on vector magnetic field measurements in the solar photosphere focuses on the issue of non-linear uncertainty propagation, which can introduce bias and hinder accurate scientific analysis. The researchers developed an iterative, linear-unbiased method as an alternative to the widely used least-squares fitting technique. This new inversion algorithm has been applied to synoptic data from the Solar Telescopes of SPVDC to compare the resulting magnetic field estimates. When similar performance metrics are used, the new inversion method demonstrates comparable results. Furthermore, an explicit uncertainty map was created to highlight areas with high estimation uncertainty. This tool has been used to analyze common features in electron density contours and HelioMap density projections. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of explicitly representing measurement uncertainty in time-series inversion outputs.

A sign problem occurs in a wide variety of particle physics and nuclear physics simulations that involve Fermions with complex exponentials in the Monte Carlo measurements. These difficulties are not present in simulations of classical spins or Bosons. We investigate the in sign problem induced instances and in some recent literature using complex valued neural networks in conjunction with auto-regressive neural network distributions. It is demonstrated that such models can bypass the sign problem in certain cases, and that they are capable of accurately solving a wide array of problems regardless of their severity. It is also proven that complex valued networks can significantly reduce the number of samples necessary to achieve the same level of precision as real valued networks.

This study investigates the behavior of topological entropy and factor complexity under free group basis changes and homomorphisms, demonstrating how these properties can be utilized to analyze the stability of subgroups within free groups. Specifically, we develop subgroups that exhibit comparable factor complexities with respect to their generating sets, which in turn enable us to explore the invariance of topological entropy under isomorphisms for a class of subgroups in a free group, as well as the monotonicity of topological complexity under inclusion for a pair of subgroups that are both of finite index in a free group.

In user experience design, recommendation systems play a crucial role, and
their effectiveness relies heavily on the quality and relevance of their
recommendations. To improve this, we have developed a novel unsupervised
cross-task generalization method called Retrieval Enhancement (R-Net). This
approach uses the relevance of past user interactions to enhance both the
current task model's learning and a reusable component that can be applied
across different tasks without requiring task-specific training data. We have
evaluated R-Net on two widely used datasets, Amazon Home-Improvement and
Amazon Fashion, using a complex setup that involves multiple binary recommendation
tasks based on product attributes. Our results show that R-Net achieves
significant cross-task generalization compared to the current state-of-the-art
unsupervised generalization methods, allowing it to effectively learn and
apply its knowledge to new tasks with limited training data.

This work is centered on the issue of hyperparameter optimization in private deep learning, which is essential for creating secure and efficient deep learning models. We have developed a framework, PHoPhI, which streamlines hyperparameter optimization in private deep learning by incorporating a robust, efficient and compact design. The PHoPhI framework is versatile and can be applied to various private deep learning projects. Experiments show that with the private federated averaging algorithm, PHoPhI successfully secures the data and accelerates model training by 10% to 20%. Furthermore, it outperforms existing methods by evaluating 3 to 5 times fewer configurations and is 3 to 8 times faster than the state-of-the-art approach. The findings from our experiments cover both controlled and real-world scenarios, validating the effectiveness and efficiency of the PHoPhI framework.

This study classify all infinite subsequences of the Cayley boolean structures of the symmetric group $S_n$ that are inclusion dense. Additionally, a specific example is identified that is not considered a subsequence of any infinite Cayley boolean structure of $S_n$.

A new approach is proposed for analyzing stellar populations that combines a
specialized clustering technique with traditional abundance analysis. This approach
utilizes Consensus Hierarchical Clustering (CHIC) to identify distinct groups of
stars based on their chemical compositions, and we demonstrate the efficacy of
this method in studying a diverse sample of 24,540 stars from the APOGEE-2
survey. By applying a two-component model that accounts for distinct stellar
populations characterized by different chemical properties, we derive an in-depth
analysis of 1 Gkpc < R$_{\rm L}$< 9 Gkpc stars using elements such as alpha, iron, magnesium, and sodium. We identify five primary stellar groups that differ
in age, metallicity, and the proportions of s-process and alpha elements. We
establish a strong correlation between specific R$_{\rm L}$-based populations
and well-documented populations defined by [Fe/H] thresholds or unique elemental
patterns, and we define a new stellar group with atypical low [Na/Fe] levels that we attribute to high-old-population stars with low angular momentum. We
further develop a method for identifying stars with unusual elemental patterns
based on residual abundances and apply it to analyze sodium and magnesium
patterns in local dwarf galaxies, revealing a wide range of stellar populations
injected into these galaxies and shaping their overall abundance distributions.

A key issue with neural machine translation models is their lack of interpretability, making it difficult to understand how they translate sentences. To address this challenge, we present a novel approach called a Spread Neural Decoder, which derives its name from the use of a Hidden Markov Model to analyze the word order of generated translations. By extracting the most influential source words and reordering them based their declining levels of impact, we can enhance the model's performance and provide a transparent explanation of the translation process. To further validate the effectiveness of this approach, we not only compare it to other neutral methods but also put forward two contrasting baseline approaches for comparison.

The rapid expansion of periodic data monitoring systems and mobile sensors has created a pressing need for an efficient flow processing engine capable of handling periodic data streams with a micro to a megabyte per second performance range. The researchers behind Facebook have developed a new architecture and implementation called LifeStream, designed to handle periodic data streams at a high speed. The LifeStream engine is based on a sophisticated pipeline that incorporates a new type of packet processing technology called packet express path. The researchers also conducted a comprehensive study and optimized cache performance algorithms, cache data structures, and management strategies to further enhance the engine's efficiency. The performance of the LifeStream engine has been found to be twenty to two hundred times faster than its predecessor, thus providing a significant improvement in the operational capabilities of periodic data monitoring and mobile sensor systems.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically timelike Bertrand curves, can only exist within specific geometric environments, and cannot be found in all space types. A categorization of these curves in a particular class of geometric environments, known as (k1,..., kn)-distribution space, is achieved and the conditions for their existence are determined.

The choice of loss function in a deep neural classifier significantly influences the model's performance in a wide range of classification tasks. Although commonly used loss functions such as softmax and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence are prevalent, alternative options exist. In this research, we investigate how the loss function influences the training of a deep neural classifier and demonstrate this impact using visualizations. A visual selfie approach is employed to make these differences apparent and easily understandable. The study employs a wide spectrum of loss functions, including those that are nonlinear. The results show that the selected loss function leads to varying model architectures that are optimized for different classification strategies. To confirm these findings, we applied a control experiment using a linear classifier. Overall, the results highlight the importance of carefully considering the loss function in the design of a deep learning classification system, as this decision has far-reaching implications for the model's structure and performance.

This research aims to advance the simulation of thermomechanical changes that occur during the crystallization triggered by strain. Strain-induced crystallization, a process in which polymer chains align and undergo thermal transitions at elevated rates of stretching, plays a pivotal role in the mechanical properties of stretched polymers. A novel simulation framework is presented, integrating various simulation approaches and models to seamlessly handle local thermal transitions, structural adjustments, and thermal and structural variations within the polymer structure. The proposed framework incorporates a coupling method that links a phase-field model of crystallization with a constitutive model exhibiting multiple relaxation mechanisms. The framework also employs a constitutive model incorporating the interaction between the phase-field and stress fields, and a moving cutoff approach is introduced to efficiently simulate regions undergoing strain-induced crystallization. The combination of these methods results in an efficient and accurate simulation framework capable of capturing the complex interplay between thermal and mechanical processes underlying the strain-induced crystallization process.

We analyze a model of a nematic superconductor with a pair-breaking magnetic field applied in the perpendicular direction. A pair-breaking field is strongly dependent on the nematic character due to the magnetization of triplet Cooper pairs with their magnetic moments oriented in the nematic d-wave symmetry. The model is mathematically expressed as a self-consistent equation for the order parameter with its components in the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and a p-x (or p-y) symmetry determined by the external field. Our study involves investigating the susceptibility in the normal state, finding the gap equation's solutions in the superconducting state and analyzing the critical temperature's behavior as it nears the normal state transition with a fixed anomaly parameter.

A differential continuous-phase modulation (CPM) detection method is introduced to reduce signal delay issues in a card reader while maintaining high data transmission speeds. The proposed method simplifies the differentially detected signal to make it compatible with conventional non-differentially detected signals. This enables the use of highly efficient detection algorithms with minimal data transmission lag. The proposed method's detection structure is analyzed and compared to existing alternatives such as differentially detected signal coherence (DCSM) and differentially detected Miller detection (DMD). Through simulation, it was found that the proposed method outperforms DCSM and DMD in data transmission speed at the same error rates. This means that a card reader using the proposed method can process transactions more quickly than those using existing alternatives.

A striking new expression for the quantum capacity of a radiation field has recently been established, which enables a precise understanding of the quantum fluctuation in particle number within a thermal distribution of particles. This understanding applies universally, regardless of the thermal distribution's specific characteristics, the statistical behavior of the particles involved, the nature of the spacetime environment, or the properties of the box containing the particles. The quantum fluctuation in particle number directly determines the compressibility of spacetime and allows for a fresh perspective on various previously derived expressions concerning this complex relationship. Furthermore, it leads to explicit, non-trivial expressions for the quantum fluctuation in particle number and the compressibility of spacetime specifically for a massless scalar field in a cubic box in spacetime, under a Planckian distribution of particles. These expressions include and extend earlier, partially motivational, derivations that also involved blackbody radiation within a cubic box in spacetime, as well as the Bose-Einstein statistics of a massless scalar field, specifically in three spatial dimensions, as recently presented.

Large-scale artificial intelligence systems increasingly rely on conditional statements
to guide their behavior, yet the effectiveness of these systems is limited by
the complex interweaving of conditions in real-world scenarios. Currently, there's
no infrastructure that allows for the creation, testing, and analysis of such
"if-then" reasoning on a broad scale. Without such tools, AI developers are
constrained in their ability to refine these systems' reasoning capabilities. To
address this challenge, we present the ATOMIC atlas, an extensive collection
of structured if-then relationships, along with robust platforms for evaluating
and visualizing these patterns. Our research has yielded over 27 million pure
if-then statements, in addition to more nuanced variations that incorporate
nuances such as pronoun usage, the interplay of multiple conditions, and condition
conjunctions. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of our atlas in supporting
various forms of conditional reasoning, including the use of pronouns, multiple
conditions, and a range of graphical methods for analyzing these patterns to
facilitate continuous improvement in AI models' reasoning capabilities.

A rapidly developing class of hybrid classical-quantum algorithms has emerged, 
designed to leverage the processing power of novel near-term hardware, including 
photonic and superconducting computers. Yet, assessing the potential advantages 
these algorithms offer over their purely classical counterparts in specific 
applications remains a challenging task. In this investigation, we developed a 
variant of the HHL-portfolio optimization algorithm tailored for use on actual 
hardware. Then, we conducted comprehensive experiments with the NISQ HHL-Portfolio 
algorithm employing a state-of-the-art hybrid HHL framework, utilizing both 
gradient descent and the variational simulated annealing method on the IBM quantum 
processor. As a result, we discovered that the NISQ HHL-Portfolio algorithm can 
achieve a 3.6% to 10.5% improvement in portfolio returns compared to the best 
achievable classical results.

To enhance data efficiency and robustness in speech processing, we investigate the potential of a simple yet effective multi-modal training approach. This strategy involves aligning short speeches with corresponding text segments in a neural network, requiring the model to accurately distinguish between correct matches and distractors. We employ a bi-directional attention mechanism to better capture the spatial relationships between the speech and text content. Notably, this multi-modal training can be conducted using only paired speech-text data, making it compatible and complementary to current transcription datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that pre-training with this multi-modal approach before fine-tuning a end-to-end speech recognition model yields significant performance gains of 3-5% on low-resource tasks with less than 5% additional training data, achieving comparable or better results than traditional loudness normalization. Furthermore, this approach is successful when applied to speaker verification, demonstrating the versatility and robustness of our model.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different measure definitions when $k_n$ grows at a rate between $n^{.5}$ and $n$. However, for rates between $n$ and $k_n$, the situation is more complex and we find that the first positions' values are not asymptotically independent and their joint probability density function, $J_n$, converges to a non-degenerate limit as the rate approaches $n$. We also examine the behavior of the second largest parking position.

Investigating superconducting nanowires, we examine a range of quantum phenomena, from coherent phase-slips to the granular nature that gives rise to the Coulomb blockade. By manipulating the gates, we can control these effects and a sudden, distinct change occurs as we transition from coherent phase-slips to incoherent phase-slips, which we can model using a simple two-state system. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability to create and destroy localised states and even a form of super-Tesla Josephson effect within the nanowire.

The challenge of predicting news videos based on text descriptions is addressed in this research, with the goal of capturing the dynamic relationships between visual and textual data in a news scenario. Our proposed solution involves a dual neural network that can infer missing visual elements and relationships between texts and visuals, combining prediction and optimization techniques to manage the complexity of the problem. We effectively manage an imbalanced dataset by focusing on predicted visual elements that correspond to relevant news. Our approach demonstrates a significant 10% improvement in performance compared to the baseline, as shown in experimental results.

An inter-level coupling effect was studied experimentally in a series of magnetically ordered states of the pyrochlore Mn2Os Mn4+ phase. By applying an external magnetic field, the positions of multiple quasi-degenerate magnetic states were mapped out with high precision. It was found that the positions of higher energy states are influenced by the location of the ground state, as a direct result of inter-level coupling. This finding is not easily observed in conventional spectroscopic methods due to their limited access to higher energy states.

The Ω-baryon, first predicted by Gell-Mann and Okun, has long held significant interest due to its unique characteristics. In 1977, its discovery at Fermilab marked a pivotal moment in physics. Since then researchers have aimed to identify additional baryons with the same -3 strangeness as the Ω-baryon, although so far, none have been observed experimentally. As far as we know,现有的 theoretical predictions primarily consist of brief descriptions. In contrast, we have made comprehensive predictions regarding the masses, quantum features, and decay widths of approximately 50 resonances situated near the $\Omega K \bar{K}$ threshold utilizing a rigorous Bayesian framework. Our results indicate that non-resonant background extensively influences the $\Omega^- \to \Lambda \bar{K} K$ decay process, particularly in the region where $3.05 < m(\bar{K} K) < 3.2$ GeV. These predictions may be explored through dedicated $\Omega^- $ baryon fixed-target experiments being planned at JPARC and other similar facilities.

Epidemiological research has commonly utilized metapopulation models, representing distinct populations as separate patches with interconnecting flows. In contrast, our framework simplifies this approach by treating the entire system as a single, homogeneously mixed population. We apply our well-stirred framework and the traditional metapopulation model to analyze infection transmission within urban bus networks. By incorporating data from RealDrive, we found that the well-stirred framework more accurately predicts observed transmission, outperforming the metapopulation model in two key performance metrics. Furthermore, our framework enables efficient exploration of intervention strategies, such as mask mandates and contact-tracing, to minimize transmission. Overall, our well-stirred framework proves to be a potent analytical tool for investigating infection transmission and potential control measures in networks of densely interconnected populations.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect (SPCE) has gained considerable interest due to its significant influence on the Spin-Hall Effect and the Spin-Orbit Torrance. In this study, we investigate the SPCE in Cobalt layers adjacent to Bismuth multilayers. Utilizing a combination of first-principles and effective Hamiltonian approaches, we observe a large spin-splitting effect in the Cobalt layers, indicative of strong spin-averaging. Furthermore, we observe an unusual inversion of subbands as a function of Co layer count. An analysis of the induced spin-averaging effect reveals that it occurs primarily at the interface and propagates through the Cobalt layers in an oscillatory manner, influenced by the thickness of the Co layers. This understanding of the spin-averaging effect opens up the possibility of engineering the transport and topological properties of heavy metal semimetal interfaces.

This paper seeks a generalized Mie-type potential solution to the $d$-dimensional fractional Schrödinger equation. Using the Jumarie fractional calculus approach, both iterative and power series methods are employed to obtain solutions.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This method, along with existing techniques, was evaluated through multiple datasets and neural network architectures. Our findings indicate that determining a variable Lipschitz constant provides the most effective generalization, surpassing existing approaches and a simple bias towards lower norms. Furthermore, our results highlight the importance of incorporating variance when dealing with Lipschitz constants and we discovered that our analysis approach can be applied to other functions that behave similarly to powers of their arguments.

We investigated the Drell-Yan production of colorless final states in third-generation gauge vector leptoquark models via $pp$ collisions at the LHC, with calculations performed at next-to-leading order in QCD. By applying the Parton Shaping method, we demonstrated that NLO QCD corrections substantially enhance the leading-order cross sections for both type-R and type-A leptoquark models, particularly in regions with high $p_T$. Additionally, we examined how various detector constraints affect the feasibility of R-parity violation in SUSY MSSM and SUSY Standard Model Extension. Graphical representations were provided for key features of phase space suppression induced by leptoquark masses and mixing angles, based on a comprehensive analysis of relevant SUSY and SRE models.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower image counts. To minimize image artifacts, our study employs multimodal learning with uncertainty estimation to assess the reliability of deep neural network (DNN) predictions, facilitating the combination of CT and low-count PET images while reducing exposure levels. We develop a two-phase network for this purpose, with phase one predicting a DNN-based enhancement of the CT scan and phase two correcting the predicted values using supervised learning, based on the predicted uncertainty. We evaluate the network's performance using metrics such as root mean square error and structure similarity, comparing results to conventional DNN prediction methods and demonstrating improved outcomes, particularly when encountering data outside the training distribution, as high-frequency components of the synthesized CT scan are better preserved when incorporating uncertainty awareness.

A linguistic approach known as Centering Theory (CT) posits that coreference links within a text are most likely to be found immediately following a sentence, with the probability of such connections decreasing as one moves further from the sentence's main focus. We investigate the validity of CT's assumptions by analyzing over 400,000 sentences from the Wikipedia corpus, revealing that while CT's general pattern holds, there are notable discrepancies, particularly when examining different parts of the corpus and comparing various entity types. Although CT's potential to guide the selection of candidate links in neural coreference resolution models is examined, we demonstrate that incorporating the concept of sentence centrality can significantly enhance the performance of a basic model.

Recently, WiFi has become an unreliable location estimation tool due to the difficulty of accurately determining the distance between devices in a network. To address this issue, this paper presents an improved method for estimating distances between access points and clients using machine learning. The proposed approach combines tree-based and ensemble models to minimize error in range estimation. Furthermore, this paper investigates the effect of noise on the effectiveness of these models and demonstrates that an ensemble model can accurately estimate range even in high-noise conditions. To support these findings, an open dataset has been created and is available for research purposes.

The beam breakup instability poses a significant challenge for superconducting beam lines and is particularly challenging in two-pass energy recovery linacs due to the necessity of isolating electron and ion beams to prevent collisions. The varying filling patterns of beams with different ion-to-electron ratios influence the threshold of beam breakup instability in a pruned energy recovery linacs. Researchers have investigated an energy recovery linacs design with a closed gap beam separator and found that higher average instabilities result from more uniform distributions of bunches. The stability thresholds for a representative two-pass design were determined for several filling patterns, revealing that less uniform distributions can increase the beam breakup threshold by a factor of 10 or more. The implications of this study may enable the use of higher beam currents in energy recovery beam lines while maintaining a safe margin from the beam breakup limit.

The paper presents the one-loop CE vertex for two gluons with a color factor of zero in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM theory. This specific vertex, which was initially described by Bartlett and Ladd in 1984, is highly relevant in calculating the amplitude for large-angle scattering of quarks and gluons. The researchers have expressed this vertex in a form amenable to use, derived its helicity components, and leveraged a previous formula to calculate the one-loop six-gluon amplitude in the limit where one gluon is much softer than the other.

We formed a comprehensive theory for heavily concentrated polymer brushes with freely jointed chains, considering arbitrarily dense solutions. By combining the concept of an effectively isolated chain (EIC) with the $3/2$ power law and by integrating the concentration profiles of brushes with slightly shorter chains sequentially, we developed an innovative approach to solving this complex problem. Moreover, it allows us to solve it for a wide range of conditions, including cases where chains can interact freely, are compressed, or are compressed and interacting. Our method enables the identification of an intermediate region in these scenarios, characterized by an effectively free chain (EFC), bridging the gap between the densely packed near-surface region and the more loosely packed far-field region. When there is compression and interaction, we found that a distinct, highly compressed, and short chain (HCSC) $3/2$ power law region exists between the EIC and EFC regions. By incorporating the HCSC region, we can accurately describe the concentration profiles of these heavily concentrated polymer brushes, achieving a precision of up to a few percent by considering only universal parameters.

A graph G is considered metric if a smallest subset of its vertices R can uniquely identify every vertex based on the distance to the set R. A smaller variant of this concept, the trimmed metric dimension, arises when a smallest subset R of the graph's vertices can uniquely identify a majority of its vertices, specifically at least ⌈|V(G)|/2⌉. A key finding from this research is that for any connected graph, the trimmed metric dimension is equal to the standard metric dimension. Nevertheless, a further examination reveals that for any integer k between 1 and the usual dimension of the graph, there exists one and only one value of the trimmed metric dimension that is strictly between k and the usual dimension, which is k + 0.5. This result, along with an illustrative example, forms the basis of the research's primary theorem.

A new set of visualizations for full-sky images from the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope is introduced, utilizing a machine learning technique known as Gaussian Process Regression to fill in data gaps and a color mapping called 'learned perceptual uniformity' to ensure accurate color representation. These improvements address limitations of previous visualization methods. In addition to methodological advancements, the paper displays enhanced versions of full-sky images from various time periods using R software. Furthermore, a dynamic, interactive application is demonstrated for exploring these visualizations with RShiny, allowing users to customize and play with different time frames. Notable astronomical objects, such as supernova remnants and active galactic nuclei, are highlighted in the visualizations to aid in user navigation. The code for implementing these new visualization methods is made available on GitHub for public use.

A convex set of functions is defined as a monarchy if all of its elements when turned into graphs lie within another, specific subset of functions known as super-modular functions. It is demonstrated that all monarchies can be characterized by a set of linear constraints and thus are optimizable using techniques for mixed整数 programming.

We are using visual color data from two Pan-STARRS1 surveys, which include data points from five different wavelength ranges, to create and analyze combinations of colors that can distinguish binary asteroids from field stars. By using machine learning techniques, we have established a method to identify and flag binary asteroids in the dataset. We first trained a random forest model on a carefully selected subset of data, which included main belt asteroids, near-Earth asteroids and distant asteroids. When we applied this model to test datasets of known origin, it successfully identified and flagged 101 binary asteroids whose status was previously unknown, many of which are located in the outer regions of the asteroid belt.

This research supplements the findings from the paper by Fu, Liu, and Su (2021), which explored the estimation and analysis of a linear regression model with an extensive network structure. The model incorporates individual components, fixed effects, and potential peer influence, utilizing the difference-in-differences technique for analysis. A crucial discovery in the study is the confirmation of peer influence's existence or non-existence through statistical methods, with an estimator created to accurately measure the influence, demonstrating strong theoretical and practical performance. The research holds particular relevance for the investigation of peer influence in extensive networks, with a novel estimator designed to replace traditional OLS methods in the analysis of peer influence equations. The research model's flexibility allows the results to be applied to various scenarios, including the examination of body composition changes and friend networks, political shifts and friend networks, and academic achievement and friend networks.

This paper presents a novel interpretation of the Leibniz Rule following the framework of fractional calculus. It offers a proof of the modified rule, expressed as the type of the fractional integral and derivative operator, by incorporating a variable-order Riemann-Liouville fractional integral and derivative into its analysis. Furthermore, it provides additional observations on this theorem, including several relevant identities, which provide valuable insights for researchers in the field of calculus.

The social interactions facilitated by artificial intelligence are limited compared to human capabilities, particularly in the area of guiding others. We introduce a new framework, inspired by the popular tabletop game Dungeons and Dragons, where the AI acts as a Dungeon Master (DM) and must guide players through the game while engaging in a conversation. We developed a method, called Learning to Converse and Guide (LCG), in which the AI learns the role of a DM through observing players' actions and making decisions. In a theoretical context, our findings demonstrate that the Intents of a Theory-of-Mind (IoTM) can enhance the effectiveness of a guided agent in specific scenarios. In a practical setting, our results show that the proposed framework and Intents of a Theory-of-Mind provide a solid foundation for a more advanced and engaging AI experience.

Understanding how knotted proteins form their native structures remains a complex challenge, since the critical role of the primary sequence in determining the arrangement of protein chains is still poorly comprehended. An incorrect model currently suggests that local folding patterns determine the formation of native structures, in contrast to evidence indicating that the overall configuration of the chain has a more substantial impact. This study introduces a topological method for identifying bending regions in knotted proteins based on their statistical properties when subjected to random entanglement. The proposed approach demonstrates that bending regions predominantly occur at structurally functional parts of the molecule, including secondary structures, dipeptide connections, and amino acids with distinctive side chains, by accurately reconstructing the bending pathways of 110 knotted proteins. Furthermore, the approach provides a topological definition of flexible and rigid segments that aligns with established biological classifications. Additionally, a list of rules is established to characterize bending regions solely from the topology of the molecule. The utility of this method is also demonstrated by analyzing the knotting characteristics of flexible and rigid segments in knotted proteins.

We define mapping category groups for symplectic mappings within a specific class of symplectic mappings that preserve the homology class in the blowups of tori, denoted as $\text{Symp}(\blom(T^n); T^n\#9 \mathbb{CP}^2_{-1})$. These mappings were analyzed by McDuff in a recent study (arXiv:2009.05550). Our definition generalizes previous concepts including symplectic mapping genus groups introduced by Hofer and the mapping genus group for contact structures that are diffeomorphic to themselves in 3-dimensional space, denoted as $S^3$.

A variation of the Nambu-Goldstone theorem is explored in both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theory. The original theorem posits that spontaneous breaking of a continuous global symmetry results in the production of a massless scalar particle. The theorem then takes on a more intricate form when the symmetry breaks in a specific way, leading to a situation where a massless vector particle is produced under certain conditions and a massless tensor particle appears when the bosons have spin one or higher. The derivation of this unusual form of the Nambu-Goldstone theorem is based on the formalism of the S-matrix.

A key advantage that large language models (LLMs) have over traditional machine learning systems is their ability to generate synthetic data, potentially high-quality examples. Despite this, LLMs have been underutilized in the field of data augmentation for supervised learning, and several studies even show that synthetic data can lead to worse model performance. In this research, we investigate the potential of LLMs to generate diverse and useful hypothetical data, specifically exploring the structure of phrasal hypotheses and their corresponding reasons and labels. By utilizing a carefully constructed hypothetical dataset, we show that synthetic data from an 8K model can effectively enhance the performance of subsequent training on a larger model, and vice versa, and that selective use of synthetic data leads to even better results. Furthermore, we find that the transfer of knowledge from an 8K model to a smaller one via our proposed methodology is significantly more beneficial than simple data augmentation, and sometimes even leads to better performance than training without any data augmentation.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene has been hindered
due to strong van der Waals interactions that limit its potential. As a result,
it is classified as a form of pinhole epitaxy, where atoms transfer directly
from the source to the substrate through small gaps in the graphene. We have
demonstrated a new approach - the remote corner configuration - enabling high-
quality epitaxial growth on graphene while restricting van der Waals interaction.
By implementing this method, we have successfully fabricated a distinct form of
corner epitaxy, effectively isolating the film from the substrate and allowing
for precise control over crystal orientation through the competition between
remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy. By epitaxially growing a Ni2MnSn
Heusler film, we have shown that the remote corner configuration can be used
to produce high-quality Heusler films with tailored physical properties by
adjusting film thickness and growth mode competition.

For any prime number $p$, this study examines $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, specifically investigating codes where $p$ does not divide the size of them. The paper begins by analyzing the properties of these codes, particularly in relation to their dual codes, and establishes the conditions under which their dual codes are $\mathbb{Z}_p$-linear. The article then proceeds to examine key characteristics of a class of codes known as quasi-cyclic codes of length $p$, focusing on their dimension, dual codes, and minimum distance. The minimum distance is bounded using the Boucher-Odoni approach. The paper also provides an in-depth study of certain classes of codes, particularly those where $p$ does not divide the size of them, and develops algorithms for creating them along with their parameters. The bookkeeping includes demonstrating that certain codes are optimal or quasi-optimal based on comparisons with existing results. The proposed methods for creating these codes are illustrated through various examples. The paper concludes by outlining several avenues for further research.

In classification tasks with multiple labels for a single data point, the common approach of balancing labels by converting multi-label labels into single-label ones can lead to incorrect or misleading outcomes. This paper highlights the inefficacy of current methods for handling multi-label datasets and puts forward two novel ways of using multi-label data to create single-label datasets that accurately reflect only one of the object's attributes. One method involves using an attribute of an object's appearance, while another relies on conceptual knowledge to define different categories. Furthermore, we examine the potential for augmenting data enhancement techniques to expand the range of attributes represented in single-label datasets.

The paper aims to provide a concise and accessible overview of the rigorous
concepts covered in Baez and Shulman's broader work, specifically focusing on the
foundations of Hilbert space theory from a categorical perspective.

We propose that high-energy gamma-rays from nearby galaxies such as M81, M51, and NGC 4258 could originate from a high-voltage gap within a magnetic confinement disk. The rapid rotation of these systems creates a energy deficit between the required electron centrifugal force and the strong magnetic force, leading to a conversion of magnetic energy and the emission of gamma-rays. We contend that the observed radio and X-ray radiation are secondary effects resulting from particle interactions, while the gamma-rays are directly linked to the gravitational and magnetic forces. Utilizing a cosmological distance measure, we calculated the expected energy spectra from these systems and discovered a degree of similarity with the gamma-rays recorded by the Fermi-LAT instrument, although there is some discrepancy with the data from the VERITAS collaboration. Moreover, our theoretical predictions suggest that the energy-flux of gamma-rays should exceed that of radio energy in certain areas, which is contrary to the characteristics of typical galaxies but consistent with M51. Consequently, we believe that high-energy gamma-rays from magnetically constricted disks represent a previously unrecognized source of such radiation.

A primary goal of point-of-care care is to quickly diagnose heart conditions through cardiac assessments, 
which require a professional to listen to heart sounds with a stethoscope and analyze them. 
Despite its simplicity, effective cardiac assessment depends on the professional's experience and is 
hindered by external noises, interference, and unusual vibrations that are common during the cardiac assessment 
procedure.  The development of an automatic heart sound categorization system that can aid in 
diagnosing heart conditions is challenging due to the need for high accuracy, low data requirements, 
and low computational complexity. To address this difficulty, this research proposes a noisy and 
distorted apical cardiogram sound classification system based on a correlation filter and a deep learning 
model. The proposed system was evaluated using noisy and distorted datasets from various sources, 
including our own, and demonstrated high accuracy rates of 94.3% to 98.3% on core segments and 93.3% 
to 96.7% on external datasets.

The proliferation of wearable devices provides promising opportunities for remote monitoring and diagnosis. However, gathering health data centrally raises significant privacy concerns. This paper introduces FedHealth, a novel federated learning framework designed to transfer knowledge in a wearable healthcare setting. It enables multiple participants to transfer data knowledge while protecting wearables' user privacy. We evaluate FedHealth using a simulated wearables data collection scenario. The framework is shown to effectively transfer knowledge and enhance the wearables' diagnostic performance using a three-way data enhancement strategy. It combats the small sample size problem effectively, yields robust results against pure federated learning approaches, and provides a privacy-preserving solution. Our research paves the way for secure and wearable healthcare applications.

This paper examines various portfolio optimization strategies that consider higher statistical properties of asset returns. We categorize and analyze multiple approaches that incorporate skewness and kurtosis, exploring the underlying formulations of each method's formulation. By expanding basic portfolio theory, we can utilize a variety of models to better reflect the complexities of financial markets. We illustrate the differences and relationships between these models through a numerical example and discuss how each method performs in an out-of-sample setting.

This paper presents an introduction to the details of the BASH system, a 
automated solution for processing software in a systematic and efficient way. 
BASH allows users to incorporate new software into its existing framework with 
relative ease, bypassing complicated programming tasks. It covers key BASH 
features, including its programming language, underlying design principles, and 
distinctive characteristics that differentiate it from other similar systems. The 
section on design principles and contrastive analysis provides an in-depth 
examination of the architecture guiding BASH's operations and its unique 
characteristics when compared to other automated processing frameworks.

This study delves into the nuances of a dynamic control problem involving
discontinuous cost functions, which depend on the trajectory of a diffusion
process, and which can occur at no cost or incur a positive cost, and
determines the optimal timing to switch between two alternative states.
Through the analysis of an example, a more comprehensive understanding of
control problems of this nature is gained, leading to a better appreciation
of the complexities of this issue, and subsequently, a new, less ambiguous
formulation of the problem is introduced, along with an associated free
boundary that reflects the nuances of the issue in a graphical format.

The characteristics of scalar leptoquark pairs produced in proton collisions at the LHC were analyzed, focusing on how their mass distributions and angular correlations can reveal asymmetries in the leptoquark coupling to quarks and lectors. These asymmetries may provide insights into new sources of violation for Lorentz and parity, which could be connected to underlying new physics. By applying different cuts to reduce background, various asymmetries can be identified with specific sensitivities to new physics, with the most effective cuts offering a sensitivity to a major source of violation far beyond what is currently achievable.

We found that in many galaxies, the low-temperature carbon monoxide (CO) lines are only partially energized compared to what would be expected based on the carbon dioxide (CI) lines' temperature. These findings suggest that subthermal stimulation of CO lines may be more common in the cool gas within galaxies than previously thought and could potentially provide insights into their gas temperatures and densities. This stimulation could result from various processes, such as collisions with hydrogen molecules, and we believe that further research is necessary to fully understand and use this phenomenon effectively.

Recently, Panshuh and Shao explored the expected distance between adjacent components in a time series under the Hamming metric, specifically for random constructions that differ by a single coordinate. However, an earlier study by Barron demonstrated that for the Hamming distance, there are scenarios where the average distance between consecutive components can be significantly influenced by a sudden change or "reconstruction" of an entire data set. In this paper, we investigate the conditions under which the distance between consecutive permutations can be influenced by such reconstruction events, aiming to characterize and calculate their influence. We have already achieved this objective for the Spearman and Kendall distances, but for the Hamming distance, the problem is more intricate, requiring a deeper analysis of the probabilities and relationships between the differences.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting low-frequency gravitational waves originating from supermassive black hole mergers and interactions. By utilizing machine learning to accelerate the computation, this study aims to produce a comprehensive catalog of precise timing signals for PTA experiments based on eccentric binary pulsar inspirals. Earlier works have highlighted the benefit of accounting for orbital eccentricity in pulsar timing data analysis, as it reduces confusion in data interpretation and enables more accurate parameter estimation. However, existing models available to analyze PTA data lack sufficient precision, particularly for large pulsar velocity inputs commonly observed. A novel, optimized set of models is presented in this paper with improved precision, including a 50% reduction in computation time at the same accuracy level compared to previous models. Furthermore, the research provides significant computation time improvements, reducing errors by up to 10 orders of magnitude for certain calculations, allowing for the creation of an highly efficient catalog of timing signals for PTA analyses.

We establish that in ASEP, the velocities of particles converge to a stochastic
evolutionary dynamic as the number of particles increases to infinity. Specifically,
we prove that the velocity process of any finite segment of ASEP on the integers,
converges to the velocity process of the ASEP with periodic boundary conditions.
Furthermore, by utilizing the inclusion-exclusion principle and the fact that
ASEP velocities are not independent, we derive the precise probability distribution
for the velocities of a set of non-interacting Bernoulli random walks.

This study examines various mathematical models developed over the last few months to analyze the ongoing global epidemic caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Beginning with an overview of fundamental concepts in epidemiological modelling, we delve into the complexities of these models and their limitations. We discuss fundamental approaches, including growth curve modelling, classical epidemiological models, and their extensions, as well as machine learning techniques and their drawbacks. A significant challenge in applying these models lies in their inherent simplicity, leading to their derisive nickname of "ghost in the machine" due to their inability to capture the full dynamics of the phenomenon under investigation.

We have theoretically analyzed the dynamics of a three-body system made of two spin-down atoms and one molecule (a diatomic particle consisting of two 'spin-up' atoms). Through precise adjustment of two key magnetic fields, we can control the loss of atoms from this three-body system by either placing the molecule in a trap with the field that causes it to decay or by reversing the field so an atom with a different magnetic property must be trapped with the defective molecule. As a result, we can effectively manage three-body collisions that lead to the emission of an electron and the creation of an atom-atom pair in different quantum states. By combining this theory with numerical simulations of the five-body recombination process, we found that under specific conditions, a spin-polarized gas of molecules can lead to a rate of five-body collisions that matches direct measurements for the first time.

Our previous work on the DNA storage protocol designed to preserve the integrity of retrieved data when new data is synthesized was limited to storing hierarchical data structures, where only the root node could be updated efficiently. To address this constraint, we present a novel scheme capable of managing non-hierarchical data and efficiently updating hierarchical data structures, including binary trees. The proposed scheme ensures that the cost of inserting new data or updating existing data grows linearly with the number of base pairs of the resulting molecule, rather than quadratically as in our previous approach, which cost function also exhibited a quadratic relationship, but with inconstant factors. The underlying strategy of the proposed scheme is based on dividing the data into smaller units, each of which can be managed independently, similar to content-addressable memory. The analysis of the proposed scheme, as well as the previously discussed 100% efficiency retrieval method, relies on a model of DNA storage that accounts for the error rates of key synthesis, sequencing, and decoding processes.

Our novel approach leverages the power of deep learning to facilitate the resolution of the shallow water equations, providing a substantial acceleration in computational time compared to traditional numerical methods. Our methodology results in a solver that is capable of handling a wide range of scenarios, from basic water depth and velocity cases to intricate geometries and complex configurations, with minimal geometric preprocessing requirements. Our rapid geometric preprocessing approach is geometrically flexible, enabling the handling of arbitrary geometries with ease. Our approach also demonstrates stability and consistency in terms of geometric approximation, ensuring high levels of accuracy and reliability in the computed results. Our model exhibits super-convergent behavior, with a convergence rate of O(h^4) in terms of the mesh size h, with a significantly higher performance in practical applications, achieving a convergence rate of approximately 3.5 in HL modules and over 5 in water depth predictions. Our evidence suggests that the observed convergence rate is likely O(h^6), with support from theoretical foundations in deep learning-based differential equations. Our model demonstrates an ability to generalize across a wide range of geometric complexities, with a consistent performance across planar, concave, and convex geometries. Our approach is also geometrically robust, with a consistent and reliable performance across a wide range of geometric configurations. Our results provide a significant advancement in the efficiency and versatility of the shallow water equations solver, with notable implications for a wide range of hydrological and oceanographical applications.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure settings to broaden the dynamic range and prevent image overexposure or underexposure. This research presents a exposure selection method and a fusion model deep learning framework for automatically producing high-quality HDR images from smartphone photographs. The proposed method leverages a mobile device's high frame rate to efficiently collect a large dataset, reducing experimentation time and resource consumption. An efficient exposure selection algorithm is proposed to systematically determine the best settings, leading to optimal results while minimizing frame usage. Furthermore, a fusion model deep learning framework is developed to integrate selected frames, introducing attention mechanisms and reducing model complexity. The proposed framework comprises two modules: one determining weighted combinations of selected frames, and another refining the combined frame. A large dataset is also created, comprising 50,000 image groups with nine scenarios, facilitating model training and testing. The proposed framework is shown to significantly surpass existing methods in subjective and objective assessments, providing a robust solution for automatic HDR creation on smartphones.

Causal profound learning (CPL) combines profound learning with causal models to enhance the effectiveness, adaptability, and interpretability of intricate profound learning models. To facilitate researchers in the field of causal learning in navigating the diverse and rapidly expanding causal profound learning landscape, we present a comprehensive survey of current methodologies, applications, and challenges of causal profound learning. We begin by categorizing existing methods into four main areas based on the intended use of profound learning: structure learning, parameter estimation, and evaluation. Next, we highlight several emerging research directions that bridge the causal learning and profound learning fields. We discuss various approaches where CCMs are integrated into multiple stages of the decision-making process, including: data management, decision-making. We examine multiple novel approaches where CCMs are employed to facilitate decision-making in rigorous and transparent ways, enabling agents to make informed choices in real-world settings across stages including: decision trees, reinforcement learning, and refinement of causal learning models. We also explore cutting-edge applications of causal learning models in real-world scenarios, including: natural language processing, vision, and multi-modal data. We review several novel approaches where the incorporation of CCMs leads to improved performance, adaptability, and interpretability of intricate profound learning models. We close the survey by outlining the challenges and limitations of current CCMs, particularly in tree-based and reinforcement learning approaches, and highlight promising research directions to address these issues.
