The Recurrence Relation Approach has been employed to derive multi-step relationships in various field models, such as Hodge decomposition and Navier-Stokes equations, resulting in efficient solver algorithms for large-scale problems. However, the approach suffers from a known limitation where single-derived relations in certain models, like the stochastic heat equation and Navier-Stokes, prove ineffective in implicit-time integration due to the absence of higher-order time derivatives. This investigation focuses on the one-dimensional stagnant random field model to address this very issue, deriving one-based recurrence relations that facilitate a non-iterative time-step update algorithm. The derived relations are subsequently extended to incorporate spatial derivatives for the stagnant random field on the unit sphere, facilitating an optimized time-step update method and enabling the efficient processing of extensive datasets in neuroimaging and cosmology.

The friction coefficient of solid foams is investigated as a function of their 
particle surface interactions and internal structure. It is demonstrated that the
value of the friction coefficient can exceed unity due to hydrodynamic effects 
performed by the liquid film. The measured friction coefficient is found to depend
on two key parameters of the foam: area fraction of the plate covered by the
foam and the surface roughness of the plate on which the foam rests. Furthermore,
it is found that the friction coefficient decreases as the roughness of the surface
increases, which is contrary to expectations for Newtonian fluids but consistent
with previous observations of granular materials and foam bulk friction.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on detecting and categorizing melanoma in images. A consistent model, utilizing a pre-trained ResNet50 for feature extraction, was developed. Initially, a neural network was trained to classify features with 5 cancer categories. To address the issue of unbalanced data and potential noise, two strategies were employed: resampling and cleaning data. Resampling balanced the dataset, while cleaning removed outlier samples based on the local regression depth (LRD) method. The local depth of images was calculated from their neighborhood and derived from the probability distribution. By integrating depth values into loss functions, the model achieved improved performance. Moreover, our approach demonstrated the effectiveness of detecting and handling anomalous data.

The steady-state Rayleigh-Benard problem within a rotating horizontal cell has a flexible membrane as its upper boundary. It is approached numerically using a spectral method based on Fourier-chebyshev expansion. The resulting equations are solved with a time-stepping algorithm. The findings demonstrate that rotation leads to the development of an inertial oscillation mode, which drives complex, flexible finger patterns in the device. It is further evidenced that the outcome includes both organic, stable finger configurations as well as chaotic oscillations of the membrane. It is also demonstrated that the flexible finger configurations can be accurately replicated using a naive drop method. It is further evidenced that increased rotation speeds lead to more complex, narrower finger configurations. It is found that the average fluid depth is directly proportional to the square of the rotation speed. The results provide a accurate prediction for the critical speed at which the membrane becomes unstable.

Scientists have identified the spectra of two isomers of cyclopentadiene, specifically ethynyl cyclopentadiene and its propargylic and necric forms, within the TMC-1 molecular cloud. This achievement overcomes earlier challenges in detecting these isomers and overcomes earlier challenges in detecting ethyl cyclopentadiene. The ethynyl and propargylic/necric isomers have an estimated abundance of 10% that of CNT and TNT variants. The absolute abundance of these isomers remains uncertain due to lack of direct measurement of the ethynyl and CNT/NT base. The estimated abundance of CN and NT bases of cyclopentadiene suggests a significant proportion of this molecule exists in saturated and monosaturated states. The ethynyl isomer's estimated abundance is comparable to vinyl and cyano variants. The neutral acetylene to cyano acetylene ratio in the TMC-1 molecular cloud is estimated to be a small fraction of one percent. The ethynyl isomer's estimated abundance may offer an alternative explanation for the TMC-1 molecular cloud's observed acetylene to cyacetylene acetylene ratio. The estimated abundance of CNT and NT isomers of cyclopentadiene may offer an explanation for the unexplained estimated abundance of TCN and TNT isomers of benzene within the TMC-1 molecular cloud.

In neural machine translation, the current model primarily processes input one word at a time, ignoring the ability to predict multiple future words simultaneously. Researchers have proposed various "focus" mechanisms to guide attention models in producing high-quality translations by emphasizing certain words in the target language. This work introduces a novel "look-ahead focus" mechanism that can predict and attend to several words before generating the next word in the sequence. This mechanism is designed to better align with the assumptions behind existing focus methods and is evaluated under an ideal scenario where it predicts and processes multiple words at a time. The proposed "look-ahead focus" algorithm is also made to work with a standard neural attention model, which it enhances by pre-emitting predicted words and using focus signals to weight attention scores. Experimental results show that this algorithm leads to notable performance gains over the standard model, yielding a +1.8 BLEU score boost. Furthermore, it demonstrates that focusing mechanisms can benefit from exploiting predicted future information, which it shares with the standard model in further experiments.

The massive amount of data generated by big data applications requires efficient processing, which can be achieved through grid computing. Despite its practical success, the underlying concepts of grid computing are not well understood due to the complexity and technical nature of related literature. This presentation will discuss the fundamental concepts behind grid computing using a simple analogy of a moving company. By comparing a company with many computers to one with a single computer, we will see how a move to a larger space with grid computing can be beneficial for processing large amounts of data, such as that generated by weather forecasting, genetic research, and financial trading simulations. This simple story will be presented in a way that allows the audience to ask questions and engage in the discussion, which is supported by actual grid computing literature.

A non-equivalent unified dark matter model has been developed, where the constituents of both dark matter and dark energy are deemed identical and subject to dissolution. These particles, referred to as $\phi$, are stable due to a specific symmetry and form the basis of a scalar field with a particular potential,pt^4/(a^4 + b^4). The parameters $a$ and $b$ in this potential give the field its non-trivial dynamics, with $b$ creating a non-shallow minimum at zero and $a$ confining the field, thus inducing a potential for slow roll inflation. The resulting dynamics of the field during its evolution lead to the generation of particles, which can account for both dark matter and dark energy. The model has been further analyzed using an effective fluid approach, and parameters have been derived that can be compared to those obtained from cosmological observations. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the model can be expressed in terms of a unified dark matter effective field theory, and it has been shown that the model occurs during an eras characterized by the expansion of the universe at a rate equivalent to matter.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains and separates new algorithms for constructing future predictive models based on reconstructed future trajectories. Contrasting our methods with existing models and past applications highlights the unique advantages of using future information. Experimental validation using real-world and synthetic data highlights the superior performance of our algorithms.

A significant finding by Furutsuki from 1980 reveals that the set of points where a one-dimensional random walk spends a non-zero amount of time is infinite. However, its applicability is limited due to its dependence on the specific starting point of the walk. In this study, we prove that the measure of the set of points where the random walk spends zero time within any given interval is bounded away from zero, regardless of the interval's length. This result is further extended to show that the random walk spends a positive amount of time at an infinitely infinite set of points within any interval. These results are crucial for the consistency of a localization approach proposed in in a recent study, where we establish the pointwise convergence of heat kernels for discrete Laplacians.

The helicon mode of the IShTAR plasma source was characterized in terms of plasma potential, density, and temperature.
Interferometric measurements revealed an increase in plasma density from the source midplane towards the limiter, with densities of 3 × 10^11 cm^-3 at the midplane and 8 × 10^11 cm^-3 near the limiters.
Energy distribution showed that 80% of the electrons were confined within a radius of 5cm from the midplane mid-sheath, with a temperature of 3.5eV and a gradient of 5eV towards the limiters.
This research aimed to determine the extent of the sheaths on the limiters and validate a 1D fluid model that yielded results of 4.5cm and 6.5cm on the thick sheaths of the outer limiters and 2.5cm on the thin sheath of the mid-sheath, respectively.

The microscopic examination of tissue samples is a routine practice in pathology, yet the in-depth analysis of cellular components within these samples has been proven challenging for human pathologists. The task is even more chemically intricate when it comes to computer vision systems. To address this difficulty, researchers have developed a gland segmentation algorithm that performs exceptionally well in the majority of images, but it tends to mistakenly identify cell clusters as glands and vice versa in certain image areas. To overcome this limitation, a new proposed network structure has been designed inspired by a popular convolutional network, specifically tailoring it to the unique scale of cells in comparison to glands. This proposed structure demonstrates superior performance and is significantly lighter in size than the current leading method.

Let F be a field of positive characteristic and let Q be a non-degenerate quadratic form over F. We consider the associated special orthogonal group O_Q and its natural action on the vector space V associated with Q. For elements x in these special orthogonal groups, we define $\epsilon(x)$ as twice the number of times a root element appears in the Jordan normal form of x, with multiplicity. We establish the existence of a split torus T whose conjugates cover O_Q and whose centralizer within the general linear group End(V) has characteristic function equal to $\Delta$, where $\Delta$ is the sum of $\epsilon(x)$ weighted by $|G|^{-1}$ over all conjugates of T for elements x in O_Q. We prove this result for the odd special orthogonal group when the dimension of V is at least seven and for the symplectic group when the dimension of V is even.

We are presenting a novel and straightforward interpretation of the GCN model that bridges the gap between traditional filter-based techniques and advanced deep learning methods, specifically in constructing and manipulating filters to improve model performance. By connecting GCNs to the concept of matched filters, we derive the GCN layer's core formula, then discuss the limitations of this approach in the context of graph-structured data, giving rise to the GGNN model. OurGGNN implementation allows for the incorporation of a non-isomorphism loss function in GGNN training, leading to enhanced GGNN performance. We successfully demonstrate the validity of our filter-based GCN theory through numerical and real-world experiments, showcasing a 5% boost in accuracy on the CiteSeck graph. Additionally, we provide an open-source code repository at https://github.com/yuxiangzhang/IntuitiveUnderstandingsofGCN.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is expanded to include a negative cosmological constant and a scalar field, all derived from a Chern-Simons action formula. This derivation implies the presence of an effective potential for the scalar field, determined by the cosmological constant. By choosing an appropriate Chern-Simons action formula, this potential can be made to accommodate various forms, including those with a positive value, which allows us to describe rotating hairy black holes and field-coated solitons.

Elastography, an ultrasonic imaging technique, visualizes the mechanical properties of tissues by relying on the displacement of tissue under certain stimuli. Two primary categories of elastography images are produced: those with axial and depth resolution and those with lateral and depth resolution. While the former type is readily achievable, the latter requires the estimation of a displacement component that is perpendicular to the ultrasound beam's direction, which is challenging due to the high variability of ultrasonic signals across different angles. To circumvent this challenge, researchers have developed sophisticated models that combine multiple beams to estimate the desired displacement, but these methods are resource-intensive and slow. To address this challenge in a more efficient manner, this study presents a novel approach called virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA), which replicates the performance of advanced methods but uses significantly fewer resources by emulating a compact sensor array. The VSSA technique achieves precise results in simulated data and demonstrates the capacity to estimate displacement in actual ultrasound images.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction are commonly taught as distinct subjects. However, there is an underlying connection that is seldom emphasized. In our work, we demonstrate how each step of an imperative algorithm can be directly correlated with a specific inference rule in natural deduction or a sequence of rules in a natural deduction system. Taking the sort of iterative range sum computation as an example, we provide a step-by-step natural deduction derivation. This approach enables us to give the concept of an invariant a concrete meaning in the context of iterative algorithms. Moreover, this framework allows us to easily obtain a full natural deduction system that captures the properties of iterative algorithms involving arrays.

In the context of dynamic data streams, we present an efficient algorithm for the $k$-centers clustering problem with updates, allowing points to be modified or removed and new points to be added within specified limits. This algorithm guarantees a solution within 3 times the optimal centers' distance with a polynomial relationship, specifically $(d^{O(1)})k^{O(1)}\epsilon$, to the ambient space's dimension. The algorithm's performance is assessed by its use of space, processing power, and the ability to handle data updates. We also provide a comparison with previous methods, highlighting the significant improvement in our approach, particularly in its dependency on the number of allowed updates.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving complex stochastic chase-evasion Markov decision decision processes by breaking them into smaller, manageable subproblems through goal-setting and value-estimation components. The goal-setting module is an approximate solution to the original MDP that yields smaller valuation MDPs, while the value-estimation module handles these valuations by combining solutions to simpler square-root-sized problems. We combine these components using a meta-actor-critic framework, and show that our hierarchical approach matches the performance of the best existing methods while providing a more balanced combination of learning components.

In our investigation, we have re-examined the accuracy of the W-boson approximation (WA) when it comes to $WW$ production at extremely high-energy muon colliders, where they can reach energies of 100 TeV. We conducted detailed analyses using full simulations of W-pair production along with initial-state radiation (ISR) for both charged and neutral initial states. By comparing the results, we found that the WA yields reliable cross-section predictions even at these extraordinary energies of 5.7 TeV and beyond. Moreover, we developed an improved (PV-WA) and a revised (PV-WR) version of the W-boson approximation, which demonstrate superior precision in predicting inclusive integrated and differential integrated cross-sections when compared to the full calculations. The performance of these approaches when applied to experimental data scenarios were also examined, revealing their potential for precise new-physics searches, with the proposed upgrades enabling enhanced sensitivity in $t\bar{t}$-production cross-section measurements with enhanced significance.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, utilizing trained models has proven beneficial for balancing exploration and exploitation, particularly when employing a unified policy to tackle multiple tasks. Despite its potential, this approach suffers from catastrophic interference, where knowledge acquired from one task can negatively impact another. This paper introduces a novel architecture, known as a modular network, which serves as a memory for separate modules that can be swapped out as needed. Each module encapsulates a distinct set of weights and corresponds to a specific learning task. Experimental evaluations using real-world environments demonstrate the advantages of this approach, showing improved performance in multi-task reinforcement learning using model-based learning and reducing catastrophic interference.

We present a formal system that embodies the limitations of formalism, semantical completeness, and proof-theoretical completeness, by deriving a sequence of theorems of increasingly broader scope over time. Thisachieves by constructing a definitional expansion of a base system similar to primitive recursive function theory, wherein the limitations first identified by G\"odel, Tarski, and Carnap, as well as by Rosser, manifest as a sequence of theorems of increasingly broader scope.

This research paper provides a substantial expansion on the "three balls conjecture," specifically for functions satisfying the Dirac equation in a Clifford setting. It effectively translates this advanced mathematical concept into a form that encompasses sub-elliptic estimates, conformal invariance properties, and Rellich-type estimates, thereby offering a comprehensive and innovative approach. A key theorem derived from this work establishes the validity of the three balls conjecture for functions in the Clifford analysis framework, utilizing estimates derived in prior research. It worth noting, however, although estimates from previous work do not directly apply due to the distinct nature of the system of equations involved, they do provide a useful guideline for developing new strategies in this area of study.

We present a novel approach to infer unknown parameters in inverse problems by utilizing a conditional generative adversarial network with a regularization term that takes into account the data. This method aims to replicate the sampling distribution conditioned on observed data, and we achieve this by formulating a regularized minimization problem that combines the KL divergence and an operator representing the problem at hand. Under certain assumptions, we prove that the solution to this problem allows for a feasible and stable approximation of the true sampling distribution, and we utilize a neural network-based algorithm to solve it. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through various experiments and visual assessments.

This research paper investigates the impossibility of invariant curves in a specific class of fractional order dynamical systems, defined by the following equations:
$$ D_t^\alpha x = f(x,y) $$
$$ D_t^\alpha y = g(x,y) $$
where the function $f$ does not equal zero. It is demonstrated that this nonexistence holds for a broad range of $\alpha$ values. It is well known in the case where $\alpha$ equals one, there is no invariant line passing through the origin with a specific slope, provided the function $f$ does not equal zero. This result is relevant to the origin stability analysis of certain classes of nonlinear fractional systems.

Analyzing 11 years of IAU VRA data for the bright pulsar B1133+16 reveals a complex interstellar medium structure around its scattering screen,无法用 a single power law model to describe, as previously indicated by radio interferometric observations. Furthermore, analyzing 11 years of ARA data shows the scattering law is not constant over time, as models with constant fraction of electrons within a given radius failed, suggesting the electrons are distributed throughout the surrounding region.

A deep convolution neural network (CNN) generative model, WaveNet, initially relied on training on spectrograms but was later adapted for direct audio waveform generation. While effective, WaveNet's scale hindered its application to pitch-based learning. This study develops Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, a variant of WaveNet that utilizes expanded convolution neural networks to capture the influence of pitch on pitch-related artifacts. By employing a unique pseudo-random sample selection method, the model learns an autoregressive model conditional on the pitch, leading to better performance in pitch-conditioned prediction tasks. In contrast to traditional CNNs, this approach results in a more dynamic and adaptive network structure that evolves with the pitch.

The theory of shadows constitutes an essential component of higher bicategorical structures, serving a similar function to that in ordinary category theory. Notably, the concept of the Morita bicategory can be fully reconstructed using the shadow functor and its natural transformation, known as the shadow. Additionally, key bicategorical properties such as the definition of equivalences and the Stacey monad, can be redefined in terms of shadows.

Cross-domain image classification models have been successfully "debiasing" images by comparing hard mining pairs and forcing certain parts of images to be classified accurately. These models, in particular, have been showing strong performance when applied to real-world scenarios, which is a significant achievement. However, the underlying reasons for their exceptional performance in "real-world" settings, which involve searching for difficult pairs manually, remain unknown, as are the characteristics of "difficult" noise regions that these models are capable of localizing. This paper aims to fill these knowledge gaps by analyzing the properties of visual noises that are difficult to classify and developing an alternative method for classifying the easy and difficult pairs in a controlled manner. It has been discovered that the models' difficulty in classifying certain noise regions is closely related to the size of these regions, as well as their contrast with the background. Furthermore, it has been proven that comparing difficult pairs effectively improves the performance of classification models and that it is possible to automatically identifying and localizing challenging and interesting regions in images that are often overlooked. These results, in particular, are relevant to the fields of robust deep learning and automatic scene classification.

The success of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in analyzing structured data has been largely driven by Euclidean embeddings, yet a significant portion of real-world datasets feature structured relationships defined by Lorentzian structures rather than Euclidean ones. We introduce a new GNN framework that effectively leverages structured data with Lorentzian embeddings, rendering it comparable to Euclidean embeddings in its expressive capacity. Our method is part of a broader, unified framework encompassing various neural network approaches for structured data. We effectively demonstrate that GNN networks in this framework can mimic the behavior of traditional E(n) neural networks. Our proposed network is efficiently trainable within a linear time complexity, scaling seamlessly with the size of the input. Our research reveals critical distinctions between Euclidean and Lorentzian neural network models. We validate our findings through numerical experiments that also show the practical applicability of our network design.

This research involves an inverse problem where the goal is to determine the porous nature of a material based on how sound behaves in a specific environment. The study uses a mathematical model that incorporates a Permeability coefficient to determine the material's properties. The material's characteristics are represented as part of a boundary condition in the acoustic model. Determining the permeability coefficient is a non-convex optimization problem, which can be solved using various mathematical techniques and algorithms. The research involves solving this optimization problem multiple times with different levels of detail, using a combination of numerical methods. The ultimate aim is to determine the shape and properties of a closed surface that, when part of an acoustically interactive environment, helps achieve a desired level of sound reduction in a specific area.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is connected to the 2K parameterization within
the two-agent delay discounting scenario from literature. This model aligns with
the Tailored Local Power Law framework and is part of a broader class of Tailored
Local laws. We demonstrate that this delay discounting model can be generalized
to a broader class of laws and utilize it to offer an explanatory approach for the
counterintuitive phenomena observed in the two-agent delay discounting situation,
specifically the potential for higher impulsivity in preferred immediate
options.

A scale-invariant extension of $R$-gauge Helvig gravity is investigated, focusing on the harmonic gauge and its variants.  By applying the harmonic gauge, the theory is reduced to a helicity-0 harmonic scalar field model.  Through non-linear gauge transformations, this model can be transformed into other gauge choices, resulting in additional harmonic gauge options.  However, the harmonic gauge is not unique, as it can be further transformed into a mixed helicity-0 and helicity-1 (transverse) model.

This research paper explores the use of Weyl and Wigner representations for canonical canonical states in a wide range of physical scenarios, ultimately leading to the derivation of specific distributional forms. By employing these quasi-probability representations, we calculate the canonical states' characteristic features and compare them to coherent states, demonstrating that the phase space area significantly influences this determination.

The notion of absolute negative temperature finds its origin in the framework of statistical mechanics, representing a rather abstract concept that does not imply a lower temperature than its positive counterpart. As the distribution of particles among various energy states approaches a particular mathematical formulation, the idea of absolute negative temperature acquires a tangible meaning. In this context, a notional reservoir of high-energy states serves to cool a system situated in a range of intermediate energy levels, effectively making absolute negative temperature an expressible and functional property.

Within the simplest "scoto-seesaw" model, we examine the dark matter behavior, the lightest extra neutrino mass, and the stability of the Higgs vacuum. In the standard linear seesaw model, these aspects are linked by a universal coupling matrix; in contrast, in the standard quadratic and scoto-seesaw models, two additional parameters, namely the neutrino effective mass scale and the new heavy neutrino mass scale, define these links. In the standard quadratic and scoto-seesaw models, we find that the dark matter scale lies significantly lower than the Planck scale, whereas the lightest extra neutrino appears at a higher energy level than its counterpart. These findings are visually supported by density plots, derived from Monte Carlo simulations, which illustrate the interconnections within the parameter space.

A fundamental aspect of solid-state physics is the interaction between electrons, which results in either the formation of sharp, overlapping electron clouds or a loss of electron character due to competition. This discussion focuses on an unusual instance where electrons with different types ($t_{2g}$ and $e_g$) compete with one another, and where their formation is gradually blended in a controlled manner in a new class of graphene-based transition metal oxides. By examining a series of oxides made with ruthenium and osmium, we have found that blending occurs smoothly, even though these metals have different levels of electron competition. This finding is not seen in traditional $t_{2g}$ electron-rich transition metal oxines made with iron group metals, where blending results are sudden. A theoretical model shows that blending results are directly related to how much a pair of electrons compete with one another. This discovery could provide a significant platform for research into understanding the behavior of materials with multiple electron competitions, by using a series of oxines to serve as precise models.

This research introduces the concept of relative quantum geometry in the context of holomorphic vector bundles over the space of relative stable maps, specifically for a pair consisting of a bundle and a target manifold. It demonstrates that the relative Kähler class defines a relative pre-quantum line bundle, which in turn leads to the relative Chern-Simons class of the bundle. Additionally, the relative Chern-Simons class is shown to be invariant under changes in the complex structure of the manifold through the use of relative Gromov-Witten invariants. The relative Hamiltonian torus action is shown to result in an insertion of relative descendents in Gromov-Witten invariants, which explains the relationship between the relative and absolute quantum geometries of the bundle and the target manifold.

This paper introduces the challenge and a dataset for illness-aware image editing, using chest X-ray data. Many current image enhancement techniques are limited, often producing over-simplified representations that result in unnatural images when attempting to represent complex conditions like tumors combined with fluid buildup or diseases like COVID. To address this, we present a dataset of 125,000 images from various disease categories, totaling 18 specific illnesses, and provide guidance on effective models and evaluation approaches for representing multifaceted illnesses, acknowledging the added complexity compared to singular conditions.

ViDaExpert is an MATLAB tool for visualizing and analyzing high-dimensional data.
It enables interactive, non-linear visualization through various 2D and 3D visualization techniques, including scatter plots, parallel coordinates, and tree maps, as well as gauge charts and area models for different purposes.
The tool also has dimension reduction capabilities via PCA and provides filtering, sorting, and statistical analysis functionalities for annotated data points via side panels.
With customizable visual features like color, shape, and size, ViDaStream is an integrated environment for effective multidimensional data analysis.
